summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965 and March 31., 1966 respectively) in the status of a 'Hindu Undivided Family. In each of the assessment assessments, the Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting, the accrued interests on the money lending investment could not be included in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee. The Wealth Tax officer sought support from a judgment of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Vedreva Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax (2) A.P. The question referred by the Tribunal was whether on the facts and circumstances of the case, the respondent was justified in including in the net wealth of the assesses interest due on accrual basis (though not realised). The High Court dismissed the appeals. Allowing the reference, HELD: Under Section 3 of the Wealth tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net income of the assesee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression 'net wealth ' is defined by cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value. Of all the assets", wherever located, belonging to the assessee on the valuation date are in excess of the aggregate amount of all the debts owed by the assessee upon the valuation dates. [310B C] In the instant case, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset.

The appellants through their legal representatives had instituted a suit for declaration and an injunction restraining the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that he was the lawful tenant of the said property and since he had not been dispossessed in accordance with law, the defen dants who were mere trespassers had been liable to be evicted. In a suit filed by the appellants it was contended that the suit was barred under Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, because (i) the respondent had threatened and deprived the appellant defendant No 2 from interfering with his possession of the suit property on the strength whereof defendant No 1 executed a deed of lease in favour of the latter effective from January 1, 1968, without his tenancy having been lawfully terminated; and (ii) the suit which was barred by res judicata as found in Order 2 rule 2(2)(3) had not come to the conclusion that 'the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit between the same parties and hence regardless of the relief claimed the second Suit was clearly barred by Res judicata. On merits, it was averred therein that he had been forcibly dispossessed from the suit premises in accordance With law the defensant defendant No: 1 executed the deed of Lease in favour thereof by defendant No, 2 effective from February 1,1968 without his contractual tenancy having being lawfully terminated.

The petitioners are engaged as carpenters 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation. They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under article 32 of the Constitution they challenged the constitutional validity of the bonus legislations. The case of the Corporation was that the unit where the petition ers were working was a factory registered under the Factories Act. It was also stated that the petitioners are supplied with the necessary tools for carry ing out their work and also working uniforms like aprons and overalls, and with the result that they execute the work in their own homes. The financial aspect of the Corpora tion was stated to be not encouraging, and indeed it was disappointing. On behalf of the petitioners it was contended: (i) The petition ants are engaged by a company incorporated under the . They cannot claim wages payable to the carpentessers in Government service; (ii) that the peti tions are comparable with the counterparts in government serv ice, (iii) that even though the petitioners ' jobs are comparable, with the counters in the Govern ment services, they cannot enforce the right to equal pay for equal work. The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Full pay for identical work will be a negation of that right. Thus the law relating to equal wages for equal Work has been practically hammered out and very little remains for further renovation.[667 A] 1.2 The law relating tOequal pay for Equal work has been almost hammered down out and too little remained for further innovation. In the light of the aforesaid principles, it could not be evaluated by the mere averments in the self serving affidavits or counter affidavits of the parties. It must be left to be evaluated and determined by expert body. The principal claim of the peti tioners therefore fails and is rejected. [665 B] 1:3 If the classification has reasonable nexus with the objective sought to be achieved, efficiency in the administration, the State would be justified in prescribing different pay scales.[668 G; 670 E F] Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. The principle of "equal pay ' for equal worked ' has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. Article 14 permits reasonable classification rounded on rational basis. It is, therefore, not impermissible to provide two different pay scale in the same cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. It would be essential that equal pay must depend upon the nature of the work done, it cannot be judged by the Mere volume of work, there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility.[670 B C] 1 :4 The principle has to be read into article 14 of the Constitu tion which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State.

The prosecution alleged that in pursuance of the conspiracy and in furtherance of their common intention they committed the murder of Sohamati on or about 10.11.1975. The charge was framed against four named persons who had been arrayed as accused 1 to 4, 6 and 7 respectively in respect of the murder by inflicting injuries on the private parts of the victims or disfiguring their faces in order to make it appear that the accused in the Manwath murders case are not the real culprits and that in furtherance pursuance of their ' common intention them committed the offence of murder of Malan, on or around 27.11 74 to 1.1.76 in the vicinity of Babultara village by inflicting stab injuries on private parts causing the private part of the victim or disfaviguring its faces in the order to pass it appear to that the said accused in Manwatath murders were not the actual culprits and had conspiracy with the other seven accused who were said to have been committed them. In the case the Sessions Judge found on a consideration of the evidence, all the seven accused not guilty of the charge of conspiracy framed under section 302 read with Section 120B I.P.C. and acquitted him of that charge, but acquitted accused 1 and 6 of charge No. 1 framed against them in respect to the murder. Accused No. 5 and 6 were convicted by the Sessions Court on the ground that they had conspired together and fabricated the deed of assignment put forward by accused 1 for availing themselves of their young girl as a member of Scheduled Tribe community and had fabricated the same before them. Accused 5 and six others filed Criminal Appeal 288 of 1980 against their conviction under Section 302 readwith Section 34 I. P.C., but acquitted them. The High Court allowed the appeal of Accused No 1 and set aside their conviction and sentence awarded to accused 6 for the murder and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for life under section 120B, I.p.C.; and confirmed their conviction by the trial court under Section 303 read with section 34, IPC. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the conviction of Accused 1 alone for conspiracy under section 148 read with s.120B, IPC is unsustainable in law as at least two persons were required for an offence of conspiracy under Section 120A I. The contentions raised by the prosecution are mainly based on the evidence of the approver P.W.1 and the retracted confession of accused 5 that he had conspired along with other seven, while accused 6 who had already been acquitted by the High Court of charge 13 as reliable and the judicial confession, Exh. 138, of accused 6 from his house and after the commission of the offence was not voluntary and reliable. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession of Accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that accused 6 had been acquitted of the charges framed under Section 301 read with 212S.P.,C. [785F G] Topandas vs State of Bombay ; and Topadas vs State Cr. A. No. 287 of 1980 decided on 23rd March, 1977, referred to. 2. The approver P W. 1 and the approver D S who had conducted autopsy on the body of the accused were amply corroborated by other evidence. viz., recovery of the blood stained razor blade, article 55, of the Accused 6 from their house; (3) evidence regarding the presence of accused 7856 along with accused 7 and PW 1 near about the scene of offence before and after commission of murder was not voluntarily made and reliable and both were corroborate by other prosecution evidence. [788G H; 786A] 3.

The appellant 's property was sought to be sold by the respondent I on August 22, 1945. The recitals in the will clearly and specifically stated that the testatrix had the knowledge of the contents of the Will; that after her death the document would remain with the appellant and it added that the plaintiff had not executed any prior will but that in case any such will has been executed by her the same stood cancelled by the execution of the present will; and on the evidence, the sound and disposing state of mind. The High Court held that even if it had found in favour of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that the will set up by him was not proved to be the last will and testament of Lakshmamma. Held, further, that after the fact that the testator was ill at Mandya and had received substantial benefit under the will and since the appellant had taken a leading part in its execution, the onus was heavy on him to remove the suspicions attending execution of a document and to establish that the executant fully understood the nature of the recitals in his preamble and the effect of the dispositions before she put her signature to the document of his own free will. The fact that after his death the testatrix has not executed anything more than an act of undue influence can not exonerate him of any possible doubt. There may be other suspicious circumstances attending on the execution. It may, however, be stated generally that a propounder of the will has to prove the due and valid execution of his will and that if there are any suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution must remove those doubts from the mind of the court by cogent and satisfactory evidence. The propounder would be called upon to show by satisfactory evidence that the document so propounded is the last Will of a free and capable testator 's signature on it when she was in a sound disposing state or of mind as required by law, courts would be justified in making a finding in favour Of the propounder.

The appellant company manufactured Arcons known as "Cinema Arc Disputes" manufactured by the appellant company, but it fell under Entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule to the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 (the Act). The entry under consideration links the taxable object with its general or ordinary use, was that they exuded their power foul light cast through the projectors on cinema screens. It was pointed out that the High Court did not consider a case in favour of the assessee. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) A perusal of Entries 1 and 4 does not effectively interpretating the entry which includes parts" as well as "accessories". [563E] (2) The word "accessory" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. There are: "supplementary or secondary to something of greater or primary importance"; "additional" and "any of several mechanical devices that assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ." [563F G] In the instant case, the High Courts have rightly held that the goods under consideration were covered by the relevant entry No.4. [562A B] (3) The judgment of the Andhra High Court is set aside and that of the Tribunal restoring the order of the Sales Tax Officer restored. [565F] The question to be decided in these cases is whether the sales of Arcon carbons and under consideration are covered by Entry No 2, relating to refrigerators, air conditioning plants covers also "component parts thereof". The High Court rightly held has that the main use of the arc carbontoons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas.

The petitioners challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966 with effect from July 1, 1985 substituting the original rule 21 by a new rule which reads as follows: "21. Rate of royalty in respect of minor minerals. . The petitioners contended that they had challenged the constitutional validity of section 15 on the ground that it infringed Articles 14 and 301 of the Constitution, and that as such their case had not been considered in the said decision. ^ HELD: 1.1 clause (b) of Article 304 has no relevance to the question in question. No restriction is being imposed on the freedom of trade of the petitioners by the levy of royalty. [414 E] 1.2 The impugned rule 21 which was substituted in the place of the former rule was invalid as it was discriminatory in character, and violative of article 14. The power exercised is legislative in nature. The authority exercising the said power has the power to make rules equi table by necessary implication. No express power need to confer on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification for purposes of implementing the policy of the Act under which the Rules are made. [435 B C] 1:3 The levy is not arbitrary, but is imposed in an arbitrary manner. The burden of establishing that the levy is unreasonably heavy is on the petitioners. It is urged that in the other States the royalty is being levied at the rate of Re. 1 per metric tonne of Black Trap and Hard Murrum from Rs.4 to Rs.7. The levy in question is not unreasonable because it was discriminat ed in character. He relied upon a decision in B.K. Trivedi & Sons and Ors. vs State of Gujarat, ; , referred to. In support of the second contention the learned counsel chal lenged that the impugned rule has been imposed in arbitrary manner; the burden of establish ing that the impost is unreasonably high, was on the peti tioners. It was lanted further that under Article 304(b) the authority which is exercising the power has to make rr equating down by necessary implications the policy underlying the Constitution if a concession is shown in favour of the poor and the down trodden, it cannot be said that the exemption or concession is invalid. According to him the Act had been passed for purposes o ring regulation and development of minerals. It cannot be contended that the said tax should be used only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose. [416 D E] 2.1 The levy was made under a law made by the Central Govern ment on which alone the restriction contemplat ed under Article 301 of Constitution regarding movement of goods from one State to another for the activity of quarrying does not involve any movement as such. [420 H] 2:2 A valid classification of persons and things for 414 purposes of imposing any obligation on them would not be violative of Article 14 provided it is a reasonable one.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village, for setting aside an order passed against him for the dissolution of the deity. The suit was resisted by the respondents on the ground that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act l Of 1925 and therefore, his case must be held to be hereditary trustees. Respondent No. 1 contended that the succession is "regulated by usage" which according to the usage of the temple the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meeting of the members of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be deemed to be a trustee within section 6 (9) Of the Act. In appeal, HELD: The office of the appellant is hereditary within the mean of s.6(9). It was not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed there was a vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. [431 G] (1) In view of section 5 (8) of Act, it is difficult to hold that the office of appellant is not hereditary within section 1(9)(i) of Madras Act. It was quite possible that for that vacancy A himself might be reelected because a retiring trustee is eligible for re elections. [427 C] In the instant case, the question to be considered in this appeal is whether the appellant holds a beneficial interest of some sort or not and does not rest upon independent title. [409 D] (2) It was well established that succession to mahantship of a mutt or religious institution is regulated by custom or usage of particular institution except where the rule of succession is laid down by the founder himself who created the endowment. In that case, although the Hinduship stands by nomination by the holder in office, it was not a hereditary succession and therefore the appellant would be a hereditary trustees because their office devolves by hereditary right or because succession to that office is specifically provided for by the terms of the deed of appointment which by their own force designate the person to succeed. There need be no blood relationship between the deceased and his successor but the right of the latter should not depend upon the choice of any individual. [414 D] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, , followed.

Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. There was no difficulty in adopting that course in this case where the testimony o sole witness has been rejected with reference to the first accused who was on the same boat with the appellant. [711G] 2.1 In a given case, there is no mention about any pool of evidence of blood even where the deceased died at No 1 in the same site plan.

There was a partnership between the partners. For the purpose of ascertaining whether on that amount tax was to be levied under the Act in the year of assessment, income from the firm was assessed before his death and section 24B was attracted, for the assessment years 1950 51, 1951 52, 1952 53 and 1953 55. The respondents were partners in a firm of solicitors. They kept its accounts on cash basis and he contended that as he had discontinued his profession in the previous year, the source had come to an end and that amounts received by him from his heirs and legal representatives after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by his heirs, and legal representative. Held, that when a person dies without furnishing a return which he has been required to furnish under the provisions of the section 22 or having furnished a return an incorrect or incomplete return then the Income Tax Officer can make an assessment of the total income of such person and determine the tax payable thereupon. Commissioner of Income tax vs E. Alfred, , that the fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 24 B and cannot be extended beyond that legitimate field field. Since the amounts sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to tax in the several years of assessment they were not liable to be assessed as income (1)[1938] 22 Tax Cases 701, referred to. Commissioner vs E., Alfed, , applied. The fiction is confined to cases provided for in the 3 sub sections Of section 24A and cannot apply beyond that permissible field field, and the fiction could not be extended by further than the liability for the income received in the subsequent year. Income tax was exigible in reference to a person 's total income after his lifetime but in the latter case the amount was received by the widow in the earlier year and it was earned by the deceased during the previous years.

Clause (3) of article 16 of the Constitution confers power to make rules prescribing, in regard to appointments to 'a) any subordinate service or post under the State Government of Andhra Pradesh or any requirement as to residence within that State. The ,st respondent State issued an order relieving the other non domicile persons appointed on or after November 1, 1956 to certain categories of posts reserved for domiciles of Telengana region, under the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959 and Rule 3 of these Rules, which was challenged by the petitioners on the ground that article 16(3) under which the Act and the Rules purport to be made had been misunderstood as conferring a power to making, a law prescribing requirement as regards residence in a part of a State: Held, that section 3 of the Public Employment and (Rquirement) Act, 1957, has an inclusive meaning and it is not necessary to express any opinion whether delegation to the Central and/or State Governments to provide by rules for the further implementing of the law made by Parliament is valid or not. It was not correct to suggest that the Constituent Assembly was thinking of residence in Districts, Taluqas, cities, towns or villages. The fact that this clause is an exception and came as an amendment must dictate that a narrow construction upon the exception should be placed as indeed the debates in the Constituent assembly also seem to indicate. Held further, that the words 'any requirement ' cannot be read to warrant something which could have been said more specifically; such words may bear upon the kind of residence or its duration rather than its location within the State. An argument based on two things viz., that the Constitution is speaking of State and Union territory, must prevail, though there may be some possibility of being overruled as unsound.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Post Office Act 1898 and in two of them, also for offences punishable under sections 467 and 471 of the Indian Penal Code and section 411 of the Penal Code. The appellant was acquitted by the Additional Sessions judge but on appeal against his acquittal in these three cases to the High Court, he confined it to the acquittal of the appellant in respect of the offences under sections 52 and 52 notwithstanding that there were compelling reasons for setting aside the order of acquittal. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the five registered letters were in the exclusive possession of the Appellant, and that the search was illegal inasmuch as it was in contravention of section 342 and that in examining the appellant the Ad ditional Session Judge did not comply with the requirements of section 343 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant : (1) that on the findings arrived at by the High court no offence under section52 had been made out; and if the High Courts took a contrary view, they should be slow in convicting the appellant for offences tinder both sections 52 or 53 of the Act and for offences thereunder. HELD: (i) The prosecution has failed to establish that these letters were found in an almirah and were with the post office, which it had to find affirmatively that the almirah contained, apart from the registered letters in question, certain other articles belonging to the appellant cannot sustain an inference that the left intact should not be in the appellant 's possession exclusively or even jointly with his father. The mere fact of possession, according to counsel, does not suffice to show that he had secreted them from the mere fact that they were found and the article entrusted was not found to have been disposed of in the manner permissible under the Act, the offence committed would be not theft but criminal breach of trust. that by itself the appellant could have no bearing on the question as to the nature of possession attributable to the Appellant. [437 E F] (ii) The mere circumstance that there was even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. It is common experience that delivery of postal articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees. The object of the provision is to prevent postal articles 'in course of disposal by post ' from being tampered with, and so the secreting, destruction etc., of postal article would defeat or tend to frustrate their delivery to the addressees. Then the High 'Court could not have held that though the locked almirah was not in the presence of the addressee, these articles were in his exclusive possession, and, therefore, the taking away of the articles by the appellant from the post offices (if that is how he came by the articles) would be theft but it has not been found in the absence of any complaint from him. [414 E F; 414 A] (iii) Whether or not there was prejudice is a question of fact and cannot be permitted to be agitated for the first time in an appeal under article 136 of the Constitution.

The appellants were the Sarpanch and the Pan chas who alleged that he had been abused, was guilty of contempt of court. The investigating officer held the charge of contempt and after considering the affidavits of the panch witnesses submitted the complaint against the appellants with the prayer to stay further proceedings pending the receipt of the stay order, namely, for default of the order. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no proper affidavit, but that the application was not accompanied by an affidavit duly sworn to or a certified copy of the High Court 's stay order; and if they wanted to ascertain the matter they should have at least stayed the proceedings for a short while and should have asked the applicant to produce a certified copies of the staying order. Held, that the High court erred in not appreciating the facts, but was exercising judicial powers, even if the Panchas stated before them that the affidavit was filed before the Panchave Panchayat he had no jurisdiction to stay proceedings before the Nyaya Panchayats when no proceeding is pending on that date, and he had hardly any jurisdiction to staying proceedings before them. It is well settled that contempt of Court is a serious matter and a High Court should be chary of finding a judicial officer guilty of breach of court for disobeying its orders unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge of the existence of the Order of the high Court ' order. The question then arises whether the Sarpanch was guilty or not. It would amount to contempt of this Court for disobey ing its orders when no Proceeding is pending before him, if he refused to accept the mere statement of the party that the Supreme Court had stayed proceedings before it.

The appellant was charged with murder of Sheo Sahai while he was being taken in custody under the provisions of an extra judicial confession made by him to a police officer and stated that he had purchased a sword from the deceased, that after hearing some noise he tried to rescue and he removed his drain stained sword. The defence was that the appellant having purchased a cycle from the appellant and deposited it stained with human blood at the Police Station on the night of the murder were sufficient to establish that it must be the appellant who committed the murder of ' Sheo Sahai or not. Held, that in view of the fact that the accused had a motive to harm Sheo Sahai he "s statement that he did commit the murder" must be rejected by the High Court on its appraisal of the evidence about the motive and purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant 's conviction and sentence. HELD: A person to be a candidate for election to the Municipal Corporation of Raipur in the month of December, 1978 under the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation Act, 1956 is defined as "the Act". The Collector published the preliminary electoral roll on September 30,1978 under Rule 4(1) of the Rules. Later on, on November 25, 1978 the poll was held and 44 persons were declared elected. Their names were, however, not published under Rule 46 of the rules in view of the interim order made by this Court. On December 31, 1978, the poll took place on December 31,, 1978. The final publication of the electoral roll under Rule 8 was done on November 16,1978 but thereafter the calendar of events was published on November 26, 1978 notifying that the poll, if necessary would take place on Dec 30, 1978 in all the 44 constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants presented a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court praying for the issue of an interim order staying the poll which had been fixed to be held on December31, 1978. On November 25 16, 1978 a large number of nominations were received by the Returning officer. It was only on December 5,1978 for the first time that a letter was addressed by petitioner No. 6 to the Collector drawing his attention to the error that had crept into the notice published under rule 4( 1) of Rules. By that time, nominations had all been received. The present petition filed in October 1978 was heard and it was dismissed on January 20, 1979. Aggrieved against this order of dismissal by the High court, Ashok Kumar Mishra and Bhagwat Singh Thakur (Petitioners No. 2 and 5 respectively in the 494 petition before the Supreme Court) were registered as appeals. One of the grounds on which the petitioners challenged the validity of the election roll was that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule (1) by the Collector and that the declaration of result of all 44 successful candidates was liable to be quashed. The petitioners were impleaded as respondents and the petition was amended by inclusion of an additional prayer that the declarations of results of election should also be quashed, and that in the course of the discussions with the press reporters on that day, the Minister had stated that he had directed the Commissioner, Raipur Division, Raipur, to entertain their claim for inclusion in the electoral Roll and he refused to receive their applications. It is not in dispute that they did not know immediately after the publication of such notice that in a period of 20 days had been mentioned in its preamble as the period within which the claims and objections could be preferred and in paragraph 7 thereof it had been stated that any such claim or objection filed beyond the prescribed period was liable, should be rejected. The Writ Petition itself was presented on December 28, 1978 when the poll had to take place On December 30, 1975, it had to be adjourned to December 30 1, 1978 at the request of the counsel for the petitioners. No satisfactory explanation was given in the behalf of the petitioners as to why they delayed the filing of the petition till December 28 and therefore it had he been stated therein that any claim or objections filed beyond December 28 should be dismissed. The respondents filed their counter affidavits. The petition was heard on December 27, 1978 and dismissed by a Division Bench.

The respondent company and its directors for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the , which is punishable under sub section (3) of that section, is punishable. Admittedly no general body meeting had been held nor could it be laid. The Full Bench was of the view that if any balance sheet was laid before a general body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general Body meeting and lay the balance sheets and profit & loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of 'the Companies Act, 1913 or section 220 of the . In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the principle accepted by this Court in the State of Bombay vs Bandhan Ram Bhandani & Ors. ; , is applicable with equal force to a prosecution under section 134 of the Companies Act and that where in a case there is no such placing of the balancesheet before the company at a general meeting, the offence u/s 134 cannot 'be committed; and that the person charged was responsible for not calling the general meeting and that section in the English Act is a composite one which lays down various requirements which are to be complied with by the Company under its first four sub clauses and sub cl. (5) is the penal sub section which penalises the failure to comply with any of the requirements contained in any of these four preceding sub sections. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The holding of the annual general meeting of the [the Stock Exchange] (in this case) was a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the Registrar. It is clear that on principle and authority it should be held that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section134. They might have been guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 but not under section 137. [416B C] Kewalram Nath Bose vs State of U.P., A.I.R. 1970 Calcutta 36, Dobey & Sons (P) Ltd. vs Registrar, Companies, Orissa, ; , distinguished. 2.1 The provision in the Indian Companies Act for laying of a balance sheet or profit and losses account before an annual general Meeting is a condition precedent to the requirement that copies thereof so laid should be filed before the Company at the general meetings. Without so laying copies could not have been sent to the Registrar and even if they were sent it would not be a compliance with the provisions.

After the Constitution of India, Parliament passed the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, which was replaced in March, 1950 by the West West Bengal special courts Act, 1949. The provisions of section 5(1) inter alia provided that a Special Court shall try such offences or classes of cases as specified in its judgment require speedier trial; and it was provided for in this sub section that the State Government might, by general or special order in writing direct, direct. "The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by them in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum and they were convicted for varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of certiorari quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that section 5 (1) was discriminatory in so far as it purported to vest in the State Govern ment an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, " whether the duration of such a case was likely to be long or not ". The High Court quashed the conviction. Held(per curiam), that section 4 (1)(v) of the Act made it manifestly clear that in exercising its powers under section 5 it had to satisfy itself, as regards matters specified in cls. (a) and (b). While considering whether there were special factors which might unduly protract its trial under the ordinary procedure a judge must look straight into the heart and regard the facts of each case concretely much as a jury would do; but since the legislature had not provided for the trial by a Special Judge in cases such as those under the procedure they could be used. A Court of conduct on the part of the judge charged with the crime cannot start a new trial after giving him certain rights to defend himself and to test his conviction either under section 3 or 4. The power of the High Courts in exercising their powers under article 227 is not wider than that of criminal courts; there are limitations beyond which they can go and even though it fails to the lot of judges to determine where those limits lie, the basis of their decision cannot be whether the Court thinks the law is for the benefit of the people or not. Where an Act does not contain any provision which provides for a speedi er trial procedure, then not with standing anything in clause (a), it has no power to issue writs under article 32 of the Constitu tion which is subject to judicial review. A judge cannot enter upon his own inquiry or hear arguments and consider argument based on irrelevant considerations which may lend support to his conclusion that the statute is ultra vires the Constitution only so far it authorising the State. In cases like these, where the law does not lay down a standard or form in accordance with which the classification is to be made, it would be the duty of the officers entrust ed with the execution of law, to make the classification in the way consonant with the principles of the constitution (3) at any rate, that part of it which authorises the State government to direct particular "cases" to be tried by a special Court according to the special procedure provided by it for the speedi 131 trial.

The assessee is a partnership firm. The Income tax officer found that in respect of which the assessee was assessable to tax for the assessment years 1962 63 to 1957 64, the Income Tax Officer issued notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961, calling upon the assessee, within 30 days from the date of service of this notice a return in prescribed form of his income. The appellant firm carried on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn. It was claimed that the partnership dated December 6, 1918 was a transfer by an instrument executed on February 7, 1948, to a limited company with effect from November 13, 1947, or February 13, 1948. The claim was rejected by the Income tax Officer and by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and also by the Tribunal on appeal to it. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 25 (4) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, which it had transferred its business to a Limited Company with effect either from November 1, 1947 or February 12, 1948; but on appeal, the Tribunal remanded the case to the Tribunal to refer certain question for determination by the High Court. In appeal to this court by the appellant firm, HELD: (i) The appellant is entitled to the benefit mentioned in section 25(4) only in respect of the money lending business. No finding in the present case is necessary because the clear fact is that the soap business was not even in contemplation much less in existence before 1922 and the same is true of the umbrella business also. It is 's case that there was no cessation of business in so far as the original business of piece goods, yarn and banking was concerned. [ abandoning the claim for relief under sub section (4), it must be held that what was intended for the money borrowed business was carried on by the assessee and which was subjected to tax under the Income Act of 1918. But, because, if the umbrella and soap business were never assessed to tax tinder the Act of 1916 they are out of the picture and in respect thereof those businesses there could be no question of the succession to the business carried on at the commencement of the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act, 1939, that is, April 1, 1939 and on which tax was charged under the Act 1918, HELD : (i)(a) There can be a succession only to the, business which had paid tax under tho Act of 1920. [118 D] (b)(ii)There cannot be a case in which both the sub sections apply at the same time because the intention is obviously to keep them separate and when sub section(4), was added, sub section 3 was amended by the addition of the words "unless there has been a succession by virtue of which the provisions of sub section 4 have been rendered applicable. [121 E; 122 C] (iii)There could be a valid gift in favour of a person who had paid 'tax under the Indian Act and, though, therefore, there was a succession within the meaning of section 25 of Act 1918 it cannot be said that the relief which was intended to for the moneys lending business would not be extended to the main business carried out at the end of the previous year. [122 E F] (iv)The partnership deed therefore clearly established that in October/November, 1937 the business that was carried was carried in by two independent Partnerships then brought into existence. It could not have been carried on until April 1 1939. There was a partition and some vilasams were allotted to the father and the rest to the son, and he was the assessee 's income. [123 G H] (v)The business which was carried out by two joint Partnerships came into existence in November/Neptember 1937, and they had come into existence on April 1. The partnership deed now stood dissolved. There is no warrant for the view that if the veil of partnership were to be found, the appellant could be denied the benefit in the year 1939 40 which was passed on April 27, 1939. It would more than disentitle the assessee to relief under subs. (4).

Held, that a partition between Khandappa and his two sons, there would be four sharers in the coparcenary property on the hypothesis of a partition of the coparcenary properties. The net effect of Explanation 1 to section 6 is the subject matter of acute controversy between the parties. Before considering the implications of Explanation I, it is necessary to remember that what Section 6 deals with is devolution of the interest which a male Hindu has in a Mitakshare coparcenary property at the time of his death. Since Explanation 1 is intended to be explanatory of the provisions contained in the section, what the Explanation provides has to be correlated to the subject matters which the section itself deals with. In the instant case the plaintiff 's suit based as it is on the provisions of Section 6, is essentially a claim to obtain a share in the interest, which her husband had at the first time of her death in the Mitakshara coparcenary property. Two things become necessary to determine for the purpose of giving relief to the plaintiff. One, her share in her husband 's share and two, her husband and their wives ' share in property under section 10 read with Rules 1 and 2 of that Section. Thus whatever be the share of the deceased in the coparcener 's wife, since there are six sharers at the date of partition of coparcenary property, each having an equal share, the plaintiff is entitled to receive a share equal to that of a son. (See Mulla 's Hindu Law,Third Edition, page 403, para 315).

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 were brought into force with effect from 27.7.60. As it came to the notice of the Government that the Indian life insur tors, with a few exceptions, were virtually controlled by few individuals who were utilising the funds of those companies to the detriment of the industry and the policyholders, the Govern ment decided to nationalise the life insurance busi ness. Accordingly the President of India promulgated the Life Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordi nance, 1956 on January 19, 1956 providing for the vesting of the management of the life Insurance business (which was called the controlled business under the Ordinance which was being carried on by any insurer in India on that day in the Central Government and providing for its management. According to section 11(2) of the Act, the Central Govern ment may, notwith standing anything contained in sub section (1), or in any other law for the time being in force, alter (whether by way of reduction or otherwise) the remuneration and conditions of service applicable to employees or any class of them is called for, the. Central Government might, if it is of the opinion that it was in the interest of the Corporation to do so, direct such employee to retire on completion of 50 years of age or at any time thereafter on giving him three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. There will be no distinction between class 111 and Class IV employees recruited to the service of the Corpora tion after 1st September 1956 by making amendments in section 11 (2) read as follows: " Section 11(1) provides that where the Central Govt. is satisfied that for the purpose of securing uniformity in the scales of remuner ation and the other terms and conditions Of service applicable, to employees of insurers whose controlled business had been transferred to and vested in it or for the purposes of reducing the remu neration payable to those employees in cases where in the interests of the corporation and its policyholders a reduction in the remuneration payable, or a revision of the other term and conditions re quired shall be called for. " The first proviso provides that notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in sub sections (1) and (2), the Central Gov ernment may, by order, made by the Central Gover ment, direct ed such employee, to retire after completion of 55 years of service or at a time thereafter, on giving notice of termination. Section 11 (3) provides for the premature retirement of an employee belonging to Class I or Class II categories appointed to the serv ice of the Corpo ration on or after 1th September, 1956.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that respondent No. 1 was a member of the Marxist Communist Party at Bhiwani. In that letter they also told the President that the Secretary had visited the Bar and inspected the Court at Charkhi Dadri on 17 February 1975. The appellants did not ask the Chief Justice, A notice was issued by the High Court in which it was stated that "if in view of this Hon 'ble Court the action of the deponent in addressing the letter in question constituted for any reason contempt of court, one would be more sorry than the deponent himself". The deponents said that if the Court was of the opinion, it was not in keeping with the well accepted role of proverbial aloofness of a Judge. The High Court also took the view that the allegations in the letter were not disputed and challenged. Allowing the appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD: 1. If on facts it appeared that the Judge did say things or matters about politics such utterances or views or observations will be the personal opinions expressed by the Judge, and, therefore, the protec tive umbrella of the court cannot be used by way of bringing the critics on the charge of contempt of Court. [244 E F] 2. If any Judge address es on political problems or controversies the Judge exposes himself to discussion by public. The reason is that the judge travels from his judicial work and descends into the arena of politics and parties. The Judge cannot in such a case take shelter behind his office if the public discusses and criticises the views expressed by him. [245 F] In the absence of any finding by the court that the appellants committed any contempt of ' Court there was never any occasion for acceptance of apology. It is not correct and proper for any Judge to accept the invitation and hospitality of any busi ness or commercial organisation or of any political party or of a club or Organisation run on sectarian, communal parochial lines. [246 C D] 3. The appeal must be allowed.

The respondent was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of certain plots in which he was the owner, and owned certain lands. In 1796 there were some disputes between Babu Ausan Singh and the Zamindars in the district and the matter was referred by the Collector of Benaras to the Board of Revenue. The dispute between the jagirdars and Zamindars ultimately ended in 1837 by a compromise between the British Government and the then Jagirdar Hat Narain Singh whereby the British government granted a pension of Rs. 36,322/8/ to Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors in perpetuity " The statements of case showed an arrangement for sharing collections. At this settlement, the revenue or land collections of Jagir became payable by the Zamindar direct to the Government and by the grant of the pension, Babu Hat Narain singh and his heirs in perpetuity were granted a right to one fourth of the land revenue collections themselves and not merely a right of receiving u money calculated on that basis. The letter dated 7th July 1837 showed an agreement for sharing collection payments. The Income tax Officer held that the amount received by the successor of Babu Harnarain Singh varied from year to year. It was further held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The source of the income was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and the when, the immediate source of income was not land or rent collections from land, it was difficult to hold that the receipt of the respondent was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Indian Income tax Act. The High Court held that from the language of the letter dated July 7, 1837, Babu Har Narayan Singh and their successors were granted in perpetuity a right, to one fifth of the lands revenue collections itself and not only a right for receiving u pearsation money calculated thereon on that footing. On appeal by certificate, HELD : The respondent was entitled to the allowance as claimed by him. [707 G] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Kunwar Sri Trivitram Narain Singha Singh, ; followed.
