In exercise of its powers under section 63(7) of the , the Central Government specified 50 as the number of 'All India Tourist Vehicle Permits ' which may be granted by the Karnataka State Transport Authority. By section 24 of the Amending Act 47 of 1978 a proviso to section 63 (7) was introduced. The appellants who were applicants for the grant of these 14 permits, filed writ petitions in the High Court. The High Court set aside the grant granting three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka state Tourism Development Corporation and instead granted three permits to private operators and increased the number to three. This order was upheld by the High court on the ground that the preference contemplated by the proviso to s 63(1), contemplated exclusion of the 'non preferred ' class if sufficient number of applicants from the preferred classes were available. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H) does not include 'any other thing being equal ' and it cannot be said that experience of running a tourist taxi taxi is a better qualification than running a Tourist bus when the question of granting permits for tourist vehicles arises. [1015 G] (2) The proviso to sec. 63( 7), which provides for preference, applies mutatis mutandis to the preference under section 47, in respect of such number of tourist vehicles as the Central government may, in cases where the said area or route lies in more than one region and the Regional Transport Authority in any other case. [ 1015 F] (3) The general scheme of the Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the case of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68 F(1) the permit had to be necessarily granted to the State Transport Undertaking, in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits.

The respondent purchased, by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company. The assessee paid some amounts towards sales tax thus determined but there remained some arrears of sales tax i.e., Rs. 3836 4 0 for 1948 49 and Rs. 1218 1 9 for 1949 50. The Sales Tax authorities took the view that it was not liable to pay sales tax due from his predecessor in title, Purushottam Raju. The respondent appealed to the Commercial Tax Officer as well as to the Board of Revenue but the appeals were dismissed. Hence this appeal by special leave. HELD: Under section 19(1) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939, which is a provision for assessment to tax of businesses which are discontinued or the ownership of which has changed. The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. There is no such provision in the Act for the period with which we are concerned in the present case, in the context and background of other sections of the Act, the word 'assess ' and 'assessment" used in s 19(2)(C) does did not include powers of recovering taxes assessed from persons other than a "dealer". There is, therefore no justification for this argument. [665 E G] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, ; , Whitney vs Commissioners of Inland Revenue, ; Harakchand section Nathu Lal vs C D. I.T.

The State of West Bengal was reorganised into the States of Bihar and Maharashtra. On March 6, 1953, the plaintiff was suspended and an enquiry held by him for having accepted illegal gratification from prisoner Ratilal Jivan. After a fuller enquiry officer made a report that the plaintiff had not demanded for copy of the report of the enquiry held against him. He was dismissed on February 2, 1955. The High Court held that there had been a breach of article 311(2) of the Constitution as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy of such report. On appeal by special leave : Held: (1) The State of Assam was not concerned with the second contention but it was a dispute between the State of Maharashtra and the State and the Union of India. In the absence of evidence that any element of relationship between a public servant and Government are based on contract within the meaning of section 60 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, the liability to pay salary, when it has been fixed, arises out of a contract to pay salaries. (2)The liability to make payment of arrears of pay does not prevail in India and it is not necessary that mens rea was lacking even in England where a special relationship exists between the Crown and its public servants. In owner or section Raphael v, , owners or sectionRaphaaliel vs State of Orissa, (1956) I All E.R. 811, followed. (3)There can be no question that the Government servant was not prejudiced by the non supply of the Report of the Enquiry Officer in its favour or against him and therefore he had to have put such arguments or material as he could dissuade the Inspector General from accepting the report before him and the tentative conclusions arrived at by the Enquiry officer were bound to influence him.

The appellant granted a lease of a coal mining right in respect of certain 150 bighas out of his terms. The lease deed recited that the northern boundary of the leasehold land was agreed to be Rs. 8/8/6/9 by the parties on the same day. In the written statement it was contended that the western boundary of their leasehold land is conterminous with the northern boundaries of the respondents ' leasehold, that as a result of a letter written by the Inspector of Mines on August 18, 1941, which the father of the appellant had, subsequently, assigned his interest to another and incorporated a map in that lease, i.e., exhibit 3(b), there was a survey of the plaintiffs ' land and that Seam Nos. The Commissioner 's report was based upon the statement that the boundary line between the two leaseholds was that found in exhibit 3 (b). In the plaint the appellants pleaded that the map translated into words indicated that the correct specification should be a line drawn from the true meeting point of the four villages. It was further alleged that the boundaries shown in exhibit III were incorrect, for there was an entry in that respect of the western boundaries to revenue records and that the respondents had knowledge of it. Held, that the suit was not barred by limitation as it was based on a mere conjecture or surmises and not upon a consideration of the relevant correspondence between the parties. The question whether the disputed extent is part of the respondent 's holding or whether the appellant 's holdings was liable to be ejected after three years had been elapsed was one of fact and fell within the scope of section 100 C. P.C., as it stood at the relevant time. The burden of proof in the former sense was undoubtedly on the respondents, but the question is whether they have adduced evidence which had the effect of shifting the onus of proof to the appellant. Talyarkhan vs Gangadas, (1918) I.A. 269, referred to.

The appellant was a saw mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. One Sankaran was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. Later, the appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. The appellant replied that he had come to the mill at the relevant time for taking his wages for that week. On July 8, 1958, Sankaran protested against his suspension and requested that in any case the departmental inquiry should be expedited. As no enquiry was held till July 2 ,1958, Sankaran again wrote to the appellant to hold the inquiry as early as possible and on July 8 and 9 1958, he was also placed under suspension pending inquiry. The same day Sankaran protested upon his reply and asked that in the meanwhile he would hold the enquiry as early and in view of his denial, a departmental inquiry would be held and he was allowed to be reinstated. In April 1958, the . appellant terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran. The industrial tribunal however directed reinstatement of Sankaran on July 2, 1958. On appeal by the Union which was granted special leave the main contention of the Union was that it would be entitled under r., 18(i) of Standing Order No. 18 (a) to dispense with the service of any employee after complying with its terms and thus completely oust security of service which had been secured to industrial employees through industrial adjudication for over a long period of time now, that no inquiry should have been held as required by r. 21 (a). Held:(i)(a) The employer could defend the action under rs. 18 in leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was misconduct and therefore the action taken under r 18 (1) was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power conferred. Further, it did not follow that the employer was empowered to take action under section 18 (i) by leading evidence. In the circumstances the Industrial Tribunal was justified in holding that the exercise of powers was colourable and it could not be said that view was incorrect. (b) The discharge was not bona fide or was a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice as it could be stated that the action was taken under rule 18(1). But the tribunal had pointed out that the employers never attempted to do so before it. It satisfied itself by producing two witnesses but withholding the important witnesses on this question was not correct.

In a suit pending in the Court of Small Causes at Ahmedabad, the parties had effectively prevented all progress in the suit during the last six years. The suit was filed against the receivers and the receiver was sought to be wound up by an injunction from interfering directly or indirectly with its rights to obtain and remain in possession of the theatre or any part thereof and to exercise its right of exhibiting "motion pictures" and entertainment etc. The Trial Court dismissed the suit but the High Court, on appeal, set aside the order passed by the Trial Court and restored that of the Trial Judge. In the course of hearing before the trial court the question whether the legal relationship arising out of the agreement dated December 1, 1960 "was barred by res judicata and estoppel under section 92 of the Evidence Act," was raised as an attempt to reopen the previous decision given by the trial judge refusing to try issues Nos. 11, 12 and 13 as preliminary issues. The objection of the Filmistan feeling dissatisfied with the order invoked the revisional jurisdiction of the High court of Gujarat under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which was entertained and elaborate arguments were advanced at the Bar. The High Court also rejected the contention that there was any bar of estoppel in law and held that evidence as to the true nature of the transaction was not admissible by virtue of section 92. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD : 1. In a suit may operate as res judicata only if there is an adjudication by the Court: the terms of section II of the Civil Procedure. The order passed or by the High 'High Court is set aside and the Trial court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [441C] 2:1. As far as the agreement of November 27, 1954, created a lease in favour of M/s. Filmisten Distributors (India) Private Ltd., and the consent decree operated as resjudicata, it was not a lease. The permission decree must be held to create a bar of res judicata as far as that question of document of November 1, 1961 created a prelimitation as far the question of the document of February 27, 1955 created a leasehold lease in respect of M 's. Film Distributors and (India). A consent decree will be held not to operate as Res judicata. [442G] 2.2 It was for the Trial Committee that question and there after the High, Court could, if the matter were brought before it by way of appeal or in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, have decided that question. The Court gave no finding expressly or by implication on the issue of resjudicata or any other issue.

The respondent was appointed as the Secretary, Zila Sainik Board, Unnao on 20th August, 1979. He was put up for a fixed term of one year w.e.f. 1st June, 1983 by an order passed in September 1981 and it was again extended upto 31st March, 1983. The terms of the appointment were substantially different. The respondent, who was not satisfied by the order, filed a Writ Petition contending that he was entitled to payment of salary upto the period he was enti tled to remain in service. In the counter affidavit it was stated that on 29th March, 1985, the services of the 1st Respondent was terminated by the issuance of a notice and payment of one month 's salary. The Single Judge allowed the Writ Petition holding that the termination order could not be sustained; and that the respondent was entitled for salary upto 30th August 1985 if he had completed 58 years of age in case the same was completed earlier during the extended period. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that during his first appointment and thereafter he was not entitled to remain on the expiry of 30th of August, 1985 unless there was a further extension, and that no further order of extention had been passed by the Governor. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that in matters where an order of termination has been made on a report which does not make out that the employer had put forward at that stage such a case. [243C] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had not urged before the High Court that he had put up at that time such a ease. His only case was that the interim order that had been made earlier on 10th July, 1986 entitled him to be reinstated in service even though there was no order of extension of service. If the respondent is really aggrieved by the judgment dated 24th March 1988 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that he did not do so.

The appellant was charged for the murder of his wife by shooting her. The deceased and P.Ws. 1, 2 and 3 were all sleeping in the room. In the middle of the night P. Ws. 1 to 3 and 3 came awakened by the cry "Amma" raising by the accused who was holding the knife. The accused dropped the knife which was then picked up by the grand mother P.W. 3, but he was later regained consciousness next morning. The daughter of P. W. 1 tried to restrain him from giving blows to two or three times. She received a stab injury. A cut injury ensued on the left side of her chest and P died as would have been caused by the knife when she was lying down. The appellant who was the brother of the deceased, raised an altercation with the deceased 's mother in law at about 10 p.m. on 18th December, 1972. P.w. 1 put his foot on the hand in which the accused was holding a knife. A synthesis was given by P.S.I. to the police station, Renigunta and reported the occurrence to him. The Sub Inspector of Police registered the First Information Report at 5 A.M., on 19th December 1972. At about 10 P.M. the father and mother in Law of the accused came there. They caught hold of the appellant and tied them to a pole in front of the house by means of a rope. Some of the villagers who had gathered there also gave a beating to the accused and the deceased intervened, and interposed herself between P. I and his brother P. R. W 3 went away. The husband and mother were seen by the cries raised by P,.Ws. 4, 5, 6 and others. He found the appellant tied him to a tree in front side of the 'house by means Of a rope and had injuries on his person. They were ultimately acquitted by the Additional Sessions Judge of the offence under Section 302 Indian Penal Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was an altercation between P;W. 1 with a knife near his left eye and P W. I who ran away at intervals. The High Court relied on the evidence of P, PWs. 1 and 2 who came to the scene soon afterwards afterwards, the High Court convicted the appellant under Section 307 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal code and sentenced him as aforesaid. In support of his contention the prosecution relied on two decisions: (a) that there is no reason to doubt the testimony of PWs. I to 3, and that the discrepancies noticed by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and that they have been unduly magnified by the learned Session Judge; (b) that as there was concurrent versions given by the prosecution and the defence and when two views were possible they the benefit of doubt should be given to the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The discrepancies in regard to which of them woke up first can only arise where it is found that the witnesses have been extremely cogent and evenly balanced views of the evidence are possible. It would not be justified in rejecting the evidence on the basis of this statement of P 'W. 11, the Medical officer who conducted the autopsy found on the dead body a stab wound on the right side. According to the prosecution the accused had made an attempt to improve his case which was originally based on circumstantial evidence so as to leave only a remote possibility in his favour; and (c) that the injuries caused to P,W. I were caused in the manner suggested by the appellant Therefore, the conviction under Section 341 read with section 34 of Indian Penal is not sustainable. [367H 359A B] Sanwat Singh vs State of Rajasthan ; , followed. In Sanwat singh & Ors. vs State Of U.P., A.I R. 1971 S.C.

Section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 defines a public servant as meaning a person falling under any of the descrip tion mentioned therein: "2. First of all that is required by this section is that a public service man denotes a person failing under any one of the two clauses namely: (a) that if he or any person on his behalf is in possession or has, at any time during the period of his office, been in possession for which the public servant cannot satisfactorily account, of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income. " In order to appreciate the question whether a Judge of the Supreme Court or a Judge o f a High Court can be prosecuted for having committed the offence of criminal misconduct as referred to in clause (e) of sub section 1 of Section 5 of the Act, it was contended by the appellant that the President is given the power to appoint Judges of the said Court as well as of the High Court by warrant under his hand and seal after consultation with such of the Judges of them of the Election Commission. It was further urged that as per Article 124(5) of the , a Judge will be liable for committing criminal misconduct within the meaning of clause (a), (b) in case of any other person, of the authority competent to remove him from his office. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove a Judge either of the courts or for that matter even to the High Courts, since the Chief Justice of India is not a vertical superior of any of them, there being no such vertical hierarchy and the Chief Election Commissioner having no power of superintendence over it mental control over him. [ charitableA] 2. The power to punish a high Court Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in Article 2 read with article 124(4) and (5) and placed before the President, a Judge cannot be removed from his post by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less then two thirds of the members of that house present and voting, has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. The said provision was substantially more than one of its terms. It also provides an additional mode of proving an offence punishable under Section 5(2) for which any accused person was being tried. [4H; 8A] 3. The distinction between a Judge and a Judge in other words, is clear from the provisions of Article 124 that where in the case of a person who commits the offence, of criminal miscon duce, as defined in the seven clauses of Sub section (1) of Section 2, there is no such requirement under any provision of furnishing particulars of his assets so as to provide a record thereof with reference to which such an opinion can be formed and there is not an vertical superior with legal authority enabling obtaining of information from the concerned Judge. It does appear that this too is a pointer in the direction that even after the 1964 amendment of the 1964 Act following the Report of the Santhanam Committee when clause (d) was inserted in sub section (I) of section 5, the Legislature did not intend to include Judges of any High Courts and the Supreme court within the purview of the enactment. [8C F; 9D] 4. The framers of the Constitution, while dealing with such constitutional functionaries, contemplated merely their removal from office in the manner provided in Article 124, clauses (4) & (5), of Article 123 of the Constitu tion, created only moral authority over his colleagues in the Supreme Courts and High Court Judges.

In an election to a seat in the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khargram Murshidabad constitutency reserved for members of Scheduled Castes. The contestants at this election were Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal, who was a member of Scheduled Caste objected to this nomination contending that Abhrajoy P kadada did not belong to any Scheduled Caste. It was alleged in the petition that Abha had secured 16,730 votes and Sudhir, 15,523 and the former was consequently declared elected. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant it was contended: (1) The election of Abhiman Pada was a general election and not an election and (2) It did not have been proved that Abana had formed a sub caste strictly so called within the Sunri caste of a caste wholly independent of the Sunras. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: Since the word "excluding" in item 40 must be read as referring to a smaller caste group within the bigger caste group of Sunris. It is only where the exclusion is by a test other than a caste group that the order expressly says so. [390 C] There was no justification for doing that. After all, the evidence led in a case may be imperfect. Suppose the evidence in another case led to the conclusion as it might conceivably do, that there was a smaller class community within the commu nate group of Sanris. [391 B C] The appeal must fail.

Section 18 (1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, provides that a landlord who receives any sum or consideration as a condi tion for the relinquishment of his tenancy of any premises by a tenant of his interest, which is made unlawful under section 15, shall be punished with imprisonment for 6 months and shall also be punhed with fine which shall not be less than Rs. 2,000 but does not mention of relinquishment or giving up possession,in general terms. Section 19(1) provides that on conviction being fined, a tenant or any person acting or purporting to act on behalf of the tenant to claim or receive any sum in respect of his occupation of any s premises would be guilty of an offence and liable to the punishment thereof specified. The section provides for the grant renewal or continuance of a lease of any tenancy by sub lease or otherwise. Section 18(1)(i) says that it is not a lawful transaction; it could only be in favour of the lessor by mutual agreement between them. The appellant was charged under section 18 (I) of Bombay Rents. Hotel and ceil Control Act for receiving money from the complainant who was the second respondent in this appeal, through one Sayed for the purpose of making necessary ar rangements about the flat occupied by him in view of his intended departure. The defence that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, was denied any aiding and abetting. The Presidency Magistrate who tried the case convicted him under section 19(2) of Act and sentenced him to imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 30,000, but he was acquitted by the charge being insufficient to prove any abetment. The High Court rejected this argument and refused special leave under article 134 (1)(c). Held, that an assignment of a tenancy is equivalent to surrender by the lessee or tenant of its rights as such. Whether abandonment of a pugree would come within the meaning of relinquishment is a question which does not arise in this case because in the face of Exhibit D there is no abandonment in the sense that the tenant disappeared from the scene altogether saying nothing and making no arrange ments about his interest and possession under the lease. Section 108, sub clause (i), of section I6, provides for tho grant, renewal or continuation of a lessee 's rights as aforesaid.

The appellants, a group of contractors, served a Charter of Demands in July 1974 on the Appellant Union for revising the wage scales of certain categories of employees and granting various other benefits. The charter of demands was questioned by them before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of their wage scales and dearness allowance and an increase from fifteen years to twenty years in the span for earning annual increments. It was contended that the escalation clause in the Equal pay structure should be removed; that the financial capacity, as a feature of the wage scale, should bericised from the correct earning capacity of each employee. The Tribunal rejected these contentions and held that it would not be possible to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. In appeal by special leave, the appellants contended that having regard to the financial position of the appellant the Tribunal erred in making the wage, retrospective and that the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat increase of Rs. 150/ to each workman in the case of others, a result wholly unwarranted, it was said, by the intent of the original award and, therefore fell beyond the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: It is not correct to contend that an illegality warranting interference under Article 136 is committed if some other method is adopted. The employer has given satisfactory reason for adopting a different mode and it cannot always be said that an illegal illegality warranting intervention under Article 226 is committed unless some other course is adopted [177B] State of Karnataka vs M/s. Patwardhan & Ors., ; , referred to. There was no justification for quashing the order dated December 22, 1978 of the Industrial Tribunal. The reasons indicated by the Tribunal were not germane as it had applied its mind in the matter and the award was made on December 20, 1978. [177H] Although there was no suggestion that there was any opposition by the company to the application for correcting the award so as to bring out what was intended. nor was there any opposition from the company, the proposed amendment in accordance with the original pay scales would yield but a very small and almost a token increase in the size of the pay packet whereas the junior employees would get a large benefit. While workmen raising industrial disputes for revision of wage scales are certainly minded about their future prospects in the matters of wages, they, surely would be more concerned with the immediate benefits according to them that is why the Industrial Tribu nal thought that an all round flat increase in dearness allowance or house rent allowance should be introduced in the dearness allowance scale or that there should be any other modification of the principle on which dearness allowance was being presently granted. The award was a composite document in which the several elements of increased wage scales, larger increments, longer span of 20 years for earning increment, dearness allowance at 10% of the basic wage, besides several other benefits, have been integrated into a balanced arrangement in keeping with what the Tribunal has found to be the financial ability of the employer. The add ment was integrated as a condition of progressive upward revision and it was not regarded as an addition to the pay of each individual workman. It could not be the case that all the employees were to get additional pay of Rs 150/ and Rs. 100/ respectively and might contend that the Tribunal had only revised the wage rates by increasing the salary on entry into the service and res judicata. The amendment made by the Industrial Tri bunal has the effect of providing a second increase, this time to each individual workmen. [174E G] In view of the increased rise in the cost of living index and for the expansion of the span from 15 years to 20 years, it is not necessary that all employees were entitled to get reduced pay of more than Rs.

The term "wages" as defined by section 2(vi) of the , includes wages fixed by an award in an industrial dispute between the employer and his employees. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal to pay to them the wages at the rate awarded, amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the respondents the said prescribed wage structure. The authority rejected the appellants ' contention that section 15 was applicable because (1) the rates of remuneration fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section .2(vi). ^ Held, that the basic assumption made by the appellant in contending that section 2 (vi) cannot take in the wages prescribed under the award is not well founded. The Court has to consider all relevant factors and if a change or revision of the terms appears to be justified it can and often enough it does radically change the terms of the contract of employment. The development of industrial law during the last decade bears testimony to the fact that on references made under section 10(1) of Industrial Disputes Act, terms of employment have constantly been examined by industrial adjudication and wherever it appeared appropriate to make changes in them, they have been made in accordance with the well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties. Further, the basic premise which has to be considered is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages payable under an award cannot fall within section 2.(vi) Of the Act before it was amended. The amendment has merely clarified what was included in the unamended definition itself. In this connection, it may be of advantage to consider the matter whether taking into account the relevant factors or, if a changed revision of its terms appears proper to make improvement in them.

The appellant was charged with the offences of forgery and misappropriation, etc. The prosecution case was that there was an application by the department for sanction to prosecute the appellant for an offence under section 409, and that on receipt of the said communication, the Director General, Home Department sent the communication stating that he had been instructed to convey sanction of the Government to his prosecution. The High Court convicted him under section 465 and section 409 I.P.C. and sentenced them to pay a specified sum of money to the appellant but maintained the conviction on the evidence that there were no sanction required for the prosecution. Held, that sanction was necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure before the appellant could be prosecuted under section409, Indian Penal Code. There is nothing in section 197 Cr. P.C., which prohibits any public servant from acting or purporting to act in the discharge of his official duties; but it would be sufficient if there was no necessary connection between them and the performance of those duties. Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli vs The King, (1948) L.R. 75 I.A. 180, Khirozan vs The State of West Bengal, ; , distinguished. A public servant can only be said to act or to purport to act, in the performanceof his official duty if his act is such as to lie within the scope of his duties; nor even every act done by him while he was actually engaged in the perform of his work would be one amounting to a crime; no sanction under section197(1), Cr.

The appellant, a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin filed its incometax return showing an income of Rs. 11,872 for the assessment year 1948 49, which its accounting year being the previous calendar year. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90 representing only the profit it made in Travancore State and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Travancore Income tax Act he refused a deduction of Rs 79,275 shown as loss from branches situate outside the State. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that the banking business of the appellant being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing and arising in that State. The High Court also upheld the decision of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner affirmed by the Income tax Appellate Tribunal but on a reference made at the instance of the Commissioner of Income tax, the High Court held the banking ' business of that appellant being the private limited company with branches in British India and other Indian States, there was no positive words which would support an interpretation in favour of the disintegration of the head " business" but took the view (1) 37 I.T.R. 266. that the object of section 24(1), was to allow a set off of profits arising under different heads and only in such cases could recourse be had to section 24 of the Act, sub section (2)(e) and if profits could not be added for the purposes of total income ' losses sustained also could not he deducted. Held, further, that the position with respect to business in British can be adjusted against profits arising from outside British India only to business or to modify the mode of computation under section 10 of the Indian Act. But then it was said that the use of these words did not circumscribe the proviso to business alone is shown by the difference in the language of the proviso. Ram Narain Sons Ltd., vs Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax (1)[1960] 2 S.C.R, 259; and Lake & Southern Mahratta Railway Co. vs Bezwada Municipality (1936) L.R 244 I.A. 268, disapproved. Arunachalam Chettiar vs Commissioner of Incometax, Madras ([1937] , Ram Narain sons Ltd., v Assistant Commissioner for Sales Tax ([1950] (5) S.T,C. 861), distinguished.

The respondent company was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace & Co., which had been,doing business in India for about 60 years. In July 1947, the private limited company raised a dispute regarding its retirement age and the contention was that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had earlier been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the age of 58 subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age to 55. Held, that in view of the finding of the Tribunal that in all the awards in recent times in the Bombay region the trend had been to fix the retire ment age at 60 years, it was not correct to say that the trend in Bombay region had been unduly fixed and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal, was in fact inaccurate. If this Court had erred in making those decisions it would be the first to admit such mistakes and to correct the error. Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd. vs The Workmen ; , followed. Duni Tom 91 (India) Private Ltd.v. The Workmen, [1960] 2 S.C.R. 888, applied. In the present case, an attempt was made on behalf of the respondent company to show that it had been not correct in stating that the pattern of age of retirement in the other concerns and the fact that in the Delhi region at least there is a general agree ment that the age should be fixed at 60, could not justify any doubt about the correctness. If an attempt appears to have been made on the basis of some decisions of this Court it would he the first for admitting such mistakes.

The first respondent, the Birla Cotton Spinning and Weaving Mills Ltd., was appointed as an Inspector of Companies for investigating the affairs of Barium Chemicals Ltd., appellant No. 1 before its incorporation in the year 1961 and to report to the Company Law Board inter alia "all the irregularities and contravention in respect of the provisions of or of any other law for the time being in force and the person or persons responsible for such irregularities and violation." The said order was made by the Chairman on behalf of the Board by virtue of the powers conferred on him by certain rules to which we shall refer later. On June 4, 1965, the company preferred a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the order. The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to a term ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . The trial court acquitted the accused on the sole evidence, that the accused was the dacoits, and convicted them accordingly. On appeal by special leave it was contended : (i) The presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case; (ii) The facts under which the one presumption or the other may be drawn would show that the persons with whom the goods were found were the dacoits themselves. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD:(i) If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small, the finding of stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. [723 G H] (ii)(a) There is a presumption that the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thief or the dacoit or the dacoitsit. In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be drew. They need not be stated here for they differ from case to case to cases, [724 E H] In what circumstances the one can presumption or "the other may he drawn, it is not necessary to state categorically in this case. It all depends upon the circumstances under which discovery of the fruits of crime are made with a particular accused. It has been stated on more than one occasion that if the gap of time is too large, the presumption that it the accused is concerned with the Crime itself gets weakened. [789 D] (b) The time interval in some cases is as short as two days and in some others it is only when the accused cannot be connected with the crimes except by reason of possession of the colour of crime that the presumption might be drawn.

The appellant firm carried on business as importers of yam and also in money lending, over a number of years. In the books of account of the appellant it was claimed that "these transactions were mere accommodations which could have no bearing to the regular business carried on by the assessee. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim holding that the debt did not arise in the course of the assessee 's business as technists and Druggists nor in the foreign business. He, however, held that on the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in law in disallowing the debt of Rs. 2,68,385 written off by the appellant in their books of accounts as irrecoverable. On a further appeal by the asses see to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal the tribunal confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The department then invoked jurisdiction under section 66(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. Of course, the appellant contended that (i) the High Court was wrong in disallowing a sum written off as irrecoverable; and (ii) that no interest was charged by the appel lant in respect of the dues at the foot of the account at the end of the Samvat Year 2007 and 2008. Held: (i). The question whether an amount written off is in respect Of loans made in the ordinary course of money lending business of the assesses is not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending transaction, nor in respect thereof. An "accommodation" advance is a neutral expression to it may be of the nature of a loan advanced in the normal course of business by a money lender; it may he wholly unrelated to the business of money borrowing or for any other business of assessee but not in the nature Of a loan. In fact, it may also be an advance the money lending or other business or of the assesee but not the nature and extent of a loans, and therefore, it is not necessary that the amount should have been sent to the Bombay firm as loans made by the partners. The statement submitted by the Tribunal is also inadequate. (ii).The Appellate Tribunal dealt with the entire material on the record in the light of the arguments advanced at the bar. On the facts found by the tribunal, which was binding on this Court, the conclusion reached by him are not supported by proper discussion of the material before it. It is true as the finding with regard to the whole of the amount of Rs 2, 68,385, there is no question oflocating any portion thereof as between the business and money lending does not affect the real question arising for decision.

In the case of banking companies or other firms, which have overdraft facilities, even if the sums are not in credit of the donor and are not with such companies or firms, gifts might be possible by adjustment of the book entries. But in the cases of non banking companies and firms, if these companies or companies do not have overdraft facility, it is not possible to make valid gift if sums or funds are not available. It was found that there were sufficient funds at the disposal of the doner by reason of which he could make the gift by such book entries.[126E E] Commissioner of Wealth Tax, West Bengal 111 vs Ashok Glass Works, and Commissioner of Gift Tax, Delhi vs Digvijaysinghji Tin Factory, ; distinguished. In the instant case before us and on behalf of the assessee, it was held that gifts were valid though not sufficient cash with firm avail able but proper book entries were made. But there was no evidence that the said sum was available with the said firm of M/s Pearls & Beads. The High Court in view of the decision of the Division Bench in the caseof Gopal Raj Swarup vs Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P., held that under section 123 of the , in case of gift of movable property, the transfer may be effected by delivery. The Court further observed that there was nothing existing goods to be part ed.

In the State of West Bengal vs Ranga Mahammad and others, AIR 1956 SC 676 this Court held that it had no power to appoint secretaries to the Government. The High Court further held that those officers had no authority to act as law secretary, superintendent and legal remembrance and member sales tax tribunal respectively on and after October 10, 1966, and they were holding and reported for duty. On April 2, 1967 a special Bench of the High Court took the view that under article 235 power to transfer judges presiding over courts vested with the High court was exclusively that of the Chief Justice. Neither the High Courts as such nor the Governor had any hand in his appointment. The State Government implemented the orders in question on March 6, 1967, and directed them to continue in the posts they were held by those officers for three years or more. In pursuance of these directions, Shri B.K. Patro was appointed as superintendent and Legal remembensible in March 1962, Shri K.P. Mohanti as Superintendent and legal clerk in March 1961. After having held that the High 's orders did not amount to a law secretary and a case was filed before the Orissa Superior Judicial Service Tribunal, which held that these officers had any authority to hold the posts in question and that they had no such authority to function as law Secretary, superintendent or legal remonstatives and member Sales tax tribunal. The Government came up by way of special leave against the order of the Orissa High Court holding that those appointments were beyond its powers. Allowing the appeal by special leave petition HELD: (1) In view of the decisions in State of Bihar vs Rangas Mahammad, ; , this Court has held in Ranga Ganisa 's case, that under Article 235 the Governor is only concerned with the appointment, promotion and posting to the cadre which power is vested in the High be exercised by the Governor under article 233 and not as with the transfer of district judges already appointed or promoted and posted to the Cadre which power was vested in him.

The lands in dispute were sold to the auction purchaser of certain property left by him under two different wills. The alienees had admittedly been in possession of the property from the date of the sales which is more than three years old by now. Admittedly, the transfers are pendente lite. In fact if the compromise was valid and binding the alienor respondent No 2 had no interest in the property to part with in view of the stipulation in the compromise that on receipt of Rs. 1 lakh he relinquished his entire interest in it. The transferees have made an attempt to hold out that there were agreements for sale prior to the compromise for which there is no acceptable evidence. The alienation are for about a purported consideration of Rs, 4 lakhs and the sale deeds indicate that the sum of Rs Rs.1 lakh had been received earlier earlier and a net amount of Rs 77,124 out of the consideration money under these documents has been paid before the registering authority. The transferee respondents have not challenged the compromise decree. Hence the suit for title and injunction. On behalf of the alienees it was contended that a similar question arose before the Orissa High Court in the case of Bhoja Govinda Maikap & Anr., AIR (1980) Ori. 108 wherein the power of the court under Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the face of an objection of one of the parties to the compromised was considered. Relying on several authorities of different High Courts and one of them the Privy Council referred to in the decision, it was held that once the Court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the court to act otherwise. It is also necessary that the compromise petition shall be accepted and in terms thereof the suit shall be disposed of and the terms of the compromise shall form part of the order to be drawn up in this Court for disposing of the special leave petition. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 There was the allegation of payment of Rs., 1 lakh to the alienee which we have not investigated and to meet the further allegation that some improvements have been made to the property which too they should have not gone into. In view of such a statement in the compromised deed signed by the parties, the second respondent had disputed the fact of payment and has, in the meantime, alienated about 81 acres of property which constitutes the subject matter of dispute to third parties. The movees have now been brought on record under order of this Court. This Court has to hold that once a court was satisfied with respect to the facts of the case it was only for the court which was satisfied by the compromise, and no other option lay without before the Court of law to act rather otherwise.

The workmen of the Company went on leave in 1 1970 to their employ ees in Bangalore and it was found that there was no practice of giving any such sick leave in the industries in Baroda or in the State of Gujarat. The company applied for leave to appeal as aforesaid, with the further direction that 'the appeal may be heard along with the identical matter (in the Alembic Glass Industries case) as also by a similar award, and the Labour Laws Review Committee and the Norms Committee of Gujarat State, which did not agree with the view taken in the case of Jyoti Ltd. Baroda, had examined the financial capacity of the two companies in question and given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit of 7 days sick leave. The Tribunal on a reference made to it at its instance gave an award awarding seven days sick Leave with full pay and dearness allowance to the workmen of that company in a year with the facility of accumulation upto 21 days, subject to the condition that the benefit would cease to apply when the benefits of the Act became available to the employees. The Company applied for and obtained special leave to appealed as aforesaid. Dismissing the appeals to this Court, HELD: 1.1. The benefit of sick leave has been allowed in the ease of glass industries by the Tribunal with reference to the reports of the National Commission of Labour, 1969, the Labour Law Review Committee, and Norms Committee. [83B] 2.1 In providing for periodical payments to an insured worker in case of sickness (sickness benefit) or for medical treatment or attendance to him or the members of his family, the legislature did not intend to substitute any of these benefits for the workmen 's right to get leave on full pay on the ground of sickness. [86C] 3.1 When a person is entitled to any of the benefits provided by the Act, he shall not be enti tled to receive any similar benefit admissible under the provisions of any other enactment and would be governed by the . [86E F] 4.2. In providing that for periodical treatment of any insured person in case o/o his sickness if certified by a duly appointed medical practitioner, it is unnec essary to mention here the several provisions in the , namely sections 47, 48 and 49 which deal with the eligibility of workmen for sickness benefit, such as to justify the rejection of the workmen. [87F G] 5.2 In providing .for periodical payment to an employees in case Of sickness (tickness) or medical treatment for attendance to be ousted by remaining absent on duty and the members 's family, it would cease not apply to cover when the benefit was allowed by the tribunal.[86A C] 6.3. It is not a bar to the demand of the workman for sick leave to the extent allowed by tho Tribunal.

The order of detention was passed on the 8th June, 1955, by which, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub clause (1) of section 3 of the , the Government of Bombay is pleased to direct that Shri Lawrence Joachim Joseph De Souza be detained. By order and in the name of Governor of Bombay, an emergency Commissioned Officer was appointed from the place where he was ordered to be detained, which included the appellant 's premises with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the relations of India with the Portuguese Government and to the security of India and to public interest. The grounds were served on him along with the order of his detention. The validity of the order is challenged by means of a writ application in the High Court, which was dismissed, while the petition for quashing the detention order was allowed. The detaining authority, exercising its power, failed to apply its mind to the existence or otherwise of the legitimate objects of detention. He relied on certain discrepancies in the affidavits of the Under Secretary and Chief Secretary filed in the Supreme Court in these proceedings. It was contended before this Court that the grounds were vague, that the claim for non disclosure of facts made by the Under secretary indicated a decision for nondisclosure by the under Secretary himself and that too at the time of filing the affidavit, on this assumption it was argued that the claims for non disclosing were invalid, and that the decision not to disclose the facts as well as the ambit of the non disclosure must be clearly communicated to the detenue at the earliest opportunity. Held:(i) The obligation to furnish particulars and duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest does not amount to denial of all particulars and the duty to afford what is contemplated by article 22 (5). The necessity for such a communication would arise only if the detenue, feeling the grounds to be vague ask for particulars. An obligation to communicate the decision cannot be implied in these circumstances. [392 F G] (ii) In the absence of any such request by the detenue the non communication of the decision could not be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to inform the detenu, at the most, it would enable him to present to the Advisory Board his difficulties in making a proper representation and to convey to it a request for obtaining the requisite particulars from the State under section 10 of the Act, for their own information and consideration.

HELD: (1) Rule 14 Of the Defence Rules, 1954 is not ultra vires the . The appellant was a Panchayat originally constituted under the C.P. & Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. On June 1, 1959, the Bombay Village Panchayats Act, 1958 (Bombay Act III of 1959) came into force in Vidharba region and by virtue of this Act the appellant was deemed to be a Panchayat under the Act. On July 14, 1961, resolution No. 2 was passed which provided that octroi duty would be imposed on the goods coming within its local limits, viz., on January 14, 1964, and February 19, 1963. The appellant 's appeal before the Standing Committee was rejected by the Samiti as per its resolution dated April 6, 1963, because the same was not filed within limitation as per the provisions of the Bombay village Panchayat Act and rule 5 of Taxes and Fees Rules 1960. On January 26, 1963 the company filed an appeal under section 124(5) before the Panchayat Samiti, Parseoni, which heard the appeal on two grounds namely, firstly that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r. 21; and secondly that the Company was not importing tea within the limits of the Panchayat for consumption use or sale. The Standing Committee allowed the appeal of the company on both grounds namely first that it is necessary for 15 years to have octroi limits prescribed with the approved by the Collector, before levying tax under r .21, and therefore the levy of octroi from April 1, 1963 was regularised and also that the tea was imported into the Panchayat limits for consumption, use or dispose of. The company thereupon filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the levy on the grounds: (1) that r. 5 of the Fees Rules was intraviress, (2) that the Standing committee had no jurisdiction to decide the appeal as it was barred by limitation because r. 4 did not require the Panchayat by which its approval to the limits and the rate at which it is to be levied and (3) that it did not fix the octroi limit in accordance with law. Held, that the essential condition precedent for the levy as provided in rr. 3 and 4 was that what the Panchayat does is to consider objections and suggestions and then finally make its choice as regards two things i.e., (1 ) the tax or fee imposed and the rates at which the same is to he levied. The word 'rate ' occurring in r. 3(b) of the Rules means the rate from which it was to be levy, (ii) the octroi will be levied from that date provided by rule and not from a date specified in the notice.

The appellants, who were the trustees of a Matam by the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act (X XIX Of 1951) had been granted in inam to the ancestor of one Ambalathadum Pachai Kandai Udayavarar temple at Eragudi. The original grant deeds were not available; but at the time of settlement of the Inams in sixties of the last century, Inam title deeds were issued in favour of the family of Pachathai Kandi Udayavar Temple at Erahgudi, from interfering with their possession while respondents 1 to 3 claimed the properties as the trustees. The appellant had alleged that the properties covered by the grant bad been granted to them by the Ruler before the advent of the British power, in India. It was denied by the appellants that they acquired title by prescription for which the original grant had been alleged to have been made according to them. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that articles 134 B and 134 C were not retrospective in operation and that if article 134 B applied, limitation should be held to have commenced from the date when the alienor either resigned his office or was removed from it. Held, that under article 134 A, the transfer made by the manager of a Hindu religious endowment is challenged on the ground that it was beyond the authority of the manager and such a challenge necessarily postulates that the transfer was effected by the Manager as manager purporting to deal with the property as belonging to the religious endowment. Where however, the transfers are made by a previous manager for a valuable consideration and the property does not belong to him and not to the Hindu Religious endowment but to the manager himself ? The evidence, on which the appellants relied, show that the alienors had been removed from management of the temple; that they had been transferred for valuable consideration.

The District Magistrate rejected the request by a detailed order dated April 21, 1979 rejecting the request of Todar Lal and Krishankumar and declaring that the cinema licence granted to Ved Gupta was valid and he was allowed to run the Apsa Theatre. However, on September 26, 1980, the Superintendent of Police reported to the district Magistrate that cinema exhibition of cinematographs in the said Cinema could not be suspended till the final decision was rendered by the Court in favour of either of the parties. On October 24, 1981, a suit filed against P and seven others by seven of the partners including Krishan Kumar for a declaration that the Cinema licence dated July 22 1969 was the property of the firm Apsra Theatre and for a prohibitory injunction restraining them from interfering with running of the cinema by the plaintiffs and also for a mandatory injunction directing them not to interfere in any manner with, the exhibition of the cinematographs which had been granted to P. On September 26 the Superintendent reported to District Magistrate that Cinema exhibition was being conducted by some persons other than the licensee and the Police had challaned the licensee under section 6 of the Act. The writ petition filed by Todar Lai Mal against the refusal by the District Magis trate was dismissed by the High Court as well as by this Court. Hence the appeal after obtaining special leave. Dismissing the Appeal, if ^ HELD: 1. It is now necessary to consider whether the licence in respect or the Aty Theatre had been given to Shri Ved Gupta in his individual capacity or as representing the partnership. [577 H] 2. The impugned order is not one suspending the licence issued in respect Of the Theatre. What was done thereunder is to suspend the exhibition which was granted to V by the licensing authori ties of the provisions of the Jammu & Kashmir ( Cinematograph), Act, and the rules and the said implied power to take all incidental steps necessary for effective enforcement of the statute.

The appellants were displaced persons with certain other properties which were not the subject matter of the present appeal. The respondent issued a notice to the appellants in respect of the lease granted under section 12 of the , representing the articles mentioned therein and calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled. The appellants, on or about July 13, 1954, came to know of this notice when the respondent considered it necessary to issue certain directions for the "preservation of the demised premises and the goods and stock in trade etc., lying in the demised Premises. These directions were given under section 10 of the Act. On February 13, 1955, the appellants appeared before the respondent and contended that he had no authority under section 11 of the . This contention was accepted by the respondent. The appellant thereupon filed an application for a writ of certiorari for quashing the notice issued to him. Held, that the Custodian had the power and had always the power to cancel leases created not merely by the evacuees but also by himself and it could be exercised " notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". The jurisdiction conferred on the evacuee under section 4 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act was a special one and that power could be exercisable only so as to override a bar imposed by any law. It could not therefore be construed as cutting down the plain meaning of the operative portion of section, namely, "notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere in any law for . the timebeing in force" meant "or any contract between the parties". The essential part of section 12 which confers power on the Custodian to cancel a lease or vary the terms thereof is unqualified and absolute. That power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could he exercised notwithstanding anything in any enactment other law in any manner for the lime being in operation" and does not include "or an contract between .the parties".

The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh determined the ceiling area and held that the land in possession of Raghubir Singh was ancestral. The Sub Divisional officer then came to the conclusion that the father and the son constitute two separate units and each one of them was entitled to get 62 Bighas and 8 Biswas only and the surplus land measuring 4 Bighas 6 Biswas and 6 Biswas may be resumed. Aggrieved by the order of the Sub Divisional Magistrate, Raghubir Singh filed a revision application before the Board of Revenue for Rajasthan which dismissed. While dismissing the writ petition, the High Court held that there was no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955 because no appeal having been filed by the State from the order, the said order became final and the Board had no jurisdiction to set aside that part of the sub Divisional Officer 's order which had gone against the State and in his favour. Hence this appeal. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court also did not go into the merits of the controversy nor did it advisable to into it and it would be for the Sub division Officer, who could decide it in the light of the observations of the Board. [728 B] 2. The Board had by its order dated 14th April, 1975 directed that the ceiling, area may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1956 and not according to the new law i,e. the Rajasthan Imposition of Ceiling on Agricultural Holding Act, 1973 (Act No. 3 of 1955) [729 B] 4. Section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 is similar to section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915. Thus there is no restriction on the powers of the board to set down the order regarding the ceiling. The provisions of the old ceiling law apply to the case but the SubDivisional Officer has committed the grave illegality on not merely ignoring the law but also ignoring the directions of the Boards of Revenue itself [730 G] 5. Under section 107, Government of Indian India Act. 1955 there was provision under Section 224 for superintendence by the High Courts ', but sub section (2) made it clear that this superintendence would not be construed as giving to the High court any jurisdiction to question any judgment of any inferior court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. [788 C] 6. It is clear from the language of Section 221 that the Board has general powers of superintendence and control over all revenue courts. It does not apply to judicial proceedings.

The first respondent, All India Reporter Limited published in addition to the law reports referred in the first paragraph of this judgment several other books commentaries, digests and manuals. But on 15 7 1981 and 3 8 1981 the Deputy Labour Commissioner wrote to the 1st respondent informing him that the proposed order of the Central Government dated 26 12 1980 was only called but there was no reply from the appellant asking it to file its written statements in the matter of non implementation of the Palekar Award as the orders of the central government made under section 12 of the Act were popularly called. The 1st Respondent also did not send a reply to the questionnaire issued by the Tribunal nor gave any evidence before the Tribunal in respect of the matters referred to therein. Instead on 15 9 1981 the 1St respondent filed a writ petition on the file of the High Court challenging the validity of the notice served on it by the Deputy Provident Fund Commissioner as well as the order made by the Central Govern ment under section 16 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 read with section 13DD of the and section 13D of the . The 1St Respondent also raised a preliminary objection that since the law report was published in Delhi which publishes the judgments rendered by the Supreme Court in Palekaran Award, it was not applicable to it. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist respondent that the law sheets were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the (Act 45 of 1955) and declared that the said law reports were not newspaper within the mischief of section2(c)(ii) of that Act. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants (i) that no ratio of decision of the Supreme court was applicable to the case, which was expressly overruled by a subsequent decision of this Court in T.V. Ramnath and Another vs Union of India and Others, [1975] Labour and Industrial Cases 488, (ii) that the refusal of the first respondent to implement the order of Central Government made on the basis of the recommendations of the Justice Palekkar Award was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983 in Civil Appeal No. 2487 of 1982, which held that the decision was not a newspaper as defined in the Act and therefore the demand made by it on the recommendations was unsustainable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It is difficult to agree with the submission made on behalf of the First Respondent that since Section 13DD and section 12DD of The Industrial Disputes (Prevention of Publication) Act 1956, are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested, the action of the 1 St respondent in issuing the impugned notice should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the First respond ent. [781C D] (2) It cannot be said that the impugned order was violative of any fundamental rights contained in Part III of the Constitution of India as the provisions of the impugned Act do not make it a newspaper. The law reports which are being published by the Ist Respondent contain information about recent events which have taken place in the Supreme Courts or in the High Courts which are public body and these matters in all are concerned to comment rather than to report; but newspapers merge into advertising Books, periodicals into books and pamphlets, both into one another; .[781D] (3) The word `public news ' is of very wide amplitude to cover the publications of both the petitioners in question. It would be inappropriate to take into consideration that information about future legal position prevailing in the country on any point decided by this Court or in High Courts cannot be given a restricted meaning to the expression `public News '.

The appellant had been described as the licensee and the licensor was seized of and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as monthly tenant. The respondent landlord filed ejectment proceedings against one 1060 Sugrabhai Mohammed, their tenant and obtained a decree. It was alleged that the licensor gave and granted his 'leave and licence ' to the licensee to use and occupy the said premises for the period of five years. The licensor had agreed to use the said shop premises as above and merely for the purpose of workshop business. The period of leave and licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 till 31st August, 1970 and it was further submitted that the licensee should not terminate the agreement earlier save and except on the ground of breach of any terms and conditions written therein. Clause 2 of the said agreement stipulated that the licence would be liable to be terminated in case. The licensee had agreed by the licensor that if he commits any default of any term and conditions or fails to pay compensation for two months, or if the licensee at any time puts up false or adverse claim of tenancy or sub tenancy the licensor shall be entitled to terminate the said licence and cancel and revoke the leave and license granted earlier. The appellant was contending that the respondent was not the owner of the workshop and also denied that he had given the workshop to respondent for conducting business. Both the trial Court and the High Court dismissed the application under Article 227 on the sole ground that there was sub tenancy by the respondent in favour of the appellant as a monthly tenant of the business with the articles and machinery belonging to the appellant and not to the respondent. The High Court allowed the special civil application. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the respondent had given his workshop for conducting a business; and (ii) the clause did not give him the status and protection of a tenant under the Rent Act but only the subtenancy as such and therefore it was recorded that as agreed 'B.C. no preliminary issue was to be framed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. By an amendment made by section 41 of the Bombay Rent Act, the appellant was entitled to be put in possession of the property. A lease involves a transfer of interest in land, Subba Rao, J., as the learned Chief Justice then was, observed in that case. This Court also referred to the well known decision in the case of Errington vs Erringtrington, ; and held that where it cannot be said that there is no error apparent on the face of the record, the error if any has to be discovered by long process of reasoning, and the trial court has taken one view which was a possible and plausible view merely because another view is attractive, the High court should not interfere and would be in error in interfering with the finding of the trial courts or interfering under Article. 227 of the Constitution over such decision. [1056H; 1057A] 2. When two views are possible and the re quirement of one view is plausible, the first Court should not interfered and would he in error while interfering with concurrent findings of facts. In deciding whether an agreement creates between the parties the relationship of landlord and tenant or merely that of licensor and licensee the decisive consideration is the intention of the parties.

The appellants were running a market as an occupation or business with high standards and that the notification directing the constitution of a Market Committee at Virudhunagar was under section 18 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933. The validity of these provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder was challenged by them before the High Court which dismissed their writ petitions. In appeal by certificate to this Court it was contended that: (i) Both the Acts were not intra vires because they had no reasonable relation to the object sought to be achieved; and (ii) the restrictions imposed by section 5 must be reasonable. Held, further, that the Act is an integrated one and its provisions are not ultra vires article 19(1)(f) or (g) of the Constitution of India. The provisions of sections 107 and 108 of the Bombay Act were protected by article 19 (1)(a) and (b). Although section 14 contemplates trade allowance it did not affect the operation of the bye law prohibiting the deduction of mahimai ' as trade allowance. It only provided that any person who was carrying on the business of purchasing or selling any commercial crop in quantities not exceeding those prescribed by Rules, made under that Act would be liable to prosecution for an offence under section 16. The exemption could be claimed if it had been earned between a specified date and a period subsequent thereto when he obtained a license. Held further, (per Sinha, C., J., Subba Rao, Wanchoo and Mudholkar JJ.): (1) Under section 18 the State Government has to establish a market committee for every notified area and in exercise of its powers under section 19 the Act the State Govt. is empowered to issue a notification declaring their intention to exercise control over the purchase and sale of such commercial crop or crops in a particular area and calling for objections and suggestions to be made within a specified time, the persons interested in that market should apply to the committee for a direction on the application by both the parties. If the person who has a licence to trade in and about the place where the market is fixed, was deprived of his livelihood which is an unreasonable restriction upon his right to do business it could still do business in the market established subject to the regulations and also did business outside the prescribed area ; and (2) the provisions of section 108 were not meant to contravene article 19. The Act was an integrated One and it regulated the buying and selling of commercial crops by providing suitable and regulated markets giving facilities for correct weigb were ensured, storage accommodation being provided they were essential services which are necessary to enable the growers of commercial crop to secure best prices for their commodities.

The appellants were charged with murder of one Ram chander Shelke. Each was convicted and sentenced to death under section 302, I.P.C. The High Court confirmed the conviction. The sentences gave rise to the present appeal by special leave. Held, that the accused had done nothing except have been present and even if it be accepted that Nilia aimed a blow, , in saving this injury to the deceased and asking him what had happened, none could find any common intention from the fact that Pandu rang, though armed with an axe, only inflicted a light blow on the scalp which did not break any of the injuries which was caused by a stick or sticks. He could have been convicted under section 326 I. P.C., but he failed to do so, and it was not sufficient to convict him under that section in the absence of anything specific the conviction could be held as correct. This is not a normal rule about circumstantial evidence, for there is no special rule of evidence for this class of case and the latter circumstances. Such an inference may arise even if one had been charged. There was no reason to depart from this practice in this case. The reason given by the High Court for treating the acquittal of the accused was not merely that the charge framed against him were not proved but also on the question of guilt, but also that of sentence. If the offences were of such a heinous nature as to attract section 302 and were of a grave character they might have caused it, though no hard and fast rule could therefore be laid down. Emperor vs Emperor, , Mahbub Shah vs King Emperor, A.I.R. 1946 P C 45 and Mahbib Sahoo vs King, Emperor, (1947) L. R. 52 I.A. 334, considered.

They would, however, be entitled to salary and other service allowances payable to them from the date from which compulsory retirement till the date Of their normal superannuation. Petition allowed. 1.2 The ratio of the decision in Tahiliani 's case is not correct and sub clause (i) to Rule 56 (j)(1) applies to Government servants in Class I or class II Service or post on substantive, temporary or offi ciating basis.
