The respondent Corporation filed a suit for the recovery of Rs. 50,000 on 27th December 1960, in respect of medical examination of his deceased wife. Before the trial court five different issues were raised. The trial court held that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation and therefore it was the case of the plaintiffs respondents that the encashment of the cheques amounted in those circumstances in law to an acceptance of the proposal of the deceased Corporation, and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11th January 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. The learned trial court further found that the accounts did not show the position alleged by the plaintiffs that the amounts paid were appropriated towards the premium and the defence of the defendant was untenable, according to them the plaintiffs had failed to prove their existence. The High Court also taken the view that the other averments in the claim that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the field officer of the Corporation that the payment of the first premium would amount to the acceptance of it were not established and even if such a representation was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules the payment could never amount to acceptance of proposal if the proposal was not otherwise accepted. Allowing the appeal by certificate, the Court HELD: (1) The High court was in error in appreciating the facts and evidence in this case. [353A] (2) The interpretation of a long time has elapsed and further in view of the fact that principal amount together with interest amounting to about Rs. 85,000/ have already been paid to the wife of the appellant and his children, the Life Insurance Corporation in this appeal does not insist on the full repayment of the sum paid and counsel on behalf of the Life insurance Corporation has stated that they would accept if half of what had been received by the respondents, namely principal together with the interest is paid back to the Corporation [354B] (3) If an insurance policy becomes effective is well settled by the authorities but before we note the said authorities, it may be stated that it is clear that the expression "underwrite" signifies accept liability under '. The dictionary meaning also indicates that. [355C D] (4) When an application so requires, the acceptance must be evidenced by the signature of one of the companies executive officers. 'Though in certain human relationships silence to a proposal might convey acceptance but in the case the of insurance silence does not denote consent and no binding contract arises until 360 the person to whom an offer is made says or does something to signify his acceptance.

The appellants, the respondents in a civil proceeding applied for an interim injunction restraining encashment of certain letters of credit opened in favour of the appellant company pending disposal of the suit. On appeal the trial court ordered to grant an interim order restraining encashment Of the letter of credit made by the appellants. The High Court observed that an order granting ex parte injunction "is final" within the meaning of article 134(1)(c) since the controversy between the parties was finally decided, it directed the filing of a complaint under section 195 Cr. P.C. against the appellant. As the suit was not filed within the period prescribed by article 133 (1) and article 133(1) the High Court set aside that order. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that before an interlocutory order could be deemed final, under article 134 (i)(c), if it amounts to final decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding ; if after the order is made, the suit or proceedings still remains to be tried and after the orders the order was not final. In appeal to this Court it was urged that the expression "final order" in section 205 (1 )(c ) means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. Dismissing the appeals, HELD : The order rejecting the injunction did not determine the rights and obligations of the respondents, and it was not contended that this Court had departed from the principle of the earlier decisions or had suggested a different test for determining the finality of orders. [707 B C] Section 205 (l) of the Government of India Act. 1935, provided that an interlocutory judgment even if it decides an issue or issues without finally determining the rights, liabilities of the defendants is not a judgment, however, a final order". The expression " final order" is in article 133, and section 105 of the Code of Civil Procedure and article133(1).

The price at the factory gate would include only the price or deemed price at that which the processed fabric would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. Rule 174 enjoins that where goods owned bythe one person were manufactured by others the information was required relating ting to the value at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, and that the persons so authorised agreed to discharge the all liabil ities under t the said act and the Rules made thereunder, the price of the grey cloth or fabric plus the value of the job work done plus the manufacturing profit and the manufacturing expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. The Department contended before the High Court that Rule 174 was applicable only to goods owned in another person, and it was not necessary to include the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. In order to explain the position it is made clear by the following illustration: if the value value of a grey cloth in the hands of the processor is Rs.20 and the value thereof of the process worked plus the manufac turing profit and his manufacturing expenses, but no other subsequent profits or expenses are.

One G had two private properties. The properties which belonged to the Math were purchased by Mahant Shivshankar Yati for Rs. 40,000 forming part of a fund left behind by his predecessor Mahant Shiv Shankar Yati. The fund passed to Mahant Shiv Birhanker Yati under a will executed in 1956, and it was provided that the income derived from the purchase of two properties had been divided into three equal shares by G. In respect of both properties, the revenue records mentioned the name of Mahant Shiv Ram and not that of Math or the deity. The High Court allowed both the appeals by its judgment and decree dated April 21, 1969. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion, the examina tions were over. The Public Service Commission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the basis of the written exami nation and select those who on the bas of the merit position was not called. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Commis sion issued notice to the successful candidates calling for interview. The said notice however did not carry any provision to re hold it. The High Court allowed the writ petitions on the ground that when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written examination and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the Written Examination from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina sion. On the other hand, the situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a re opening interview of any eligible candidate on the par tic basis of his written examiner al examination and select Those who on that basis were not called for interview but were also finally selected. When the vacancies were known and advertised, respondent 's appointments were cancelled, it was no justi fied for canceling the entire selection examination and asking re holding of it. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, the Court. ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant State Public Service Devel tration should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not suffer.

The appellant brought the suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches, one in Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State and that he, as mahant in charge of the Shiromani Dera, at Patiala had the right to manage the properties attached to the Dera. The prayer in the plaint was for recovery of possession of the Dakhera and the properties annexed to it. Som Dass, the defendant, contended, that the Dhoh at Lande was an independent Dera and that his appointment as mahants was not open to challenge him. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal by the defendant decree was reversed and the appellant 's suit was dismissed. However, it was restored. the respondent filed a second appeal before the High Court contending, that there had been no abatement of the appeal even if he was not impleaded within the period prescribed as he claimed to represent the dera as its duly elected Chela. The High Court, on reference, took the view that after the death of Som Dass his Shiam Dass as his Chela 'inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a dispute was raised about such rights then the appellant was bound to bring on record the legal representatives of the deceased within the time prescribed by law. It further held that after Som Dass died, the interest which was the subject matter of the suit, devolved upon Shiam Das as he was elected to be the Mahant of the Dharwara and the appeal could be continued under Q. 22 r. 10 (1). Dismissing the appeal in part, ^ HELD: 1. The suit against Som Dass was not in his personal capacity but in his capacity as de facto mahant. [490 D] 2. A suit which is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, r.10 and not Rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason. Order 22 R, rr. 10, 17 and 30 are not confined to devolution of interest of a party by death, it also applies if the head of the mutt or manager of the temple resigns his office or is removed from office. In such a case, the successor to the head or to the manager of a temple may be substituted as a party under this rule. [49 F G] 3. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in the rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject matters of the Suit and the interest is the interest. of the person who was the party to the suit.[490 D E] 4. A right has to have recourse to the provisions contained in Order 22 r, r 10 during the pendency of a suit but that suit may be continued against the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court. When a suit is brought on by or between a person who claims (though illegally according to the appellant) as ma Muttor of the respondent after the deceased, the Court has no jurisdiction to set aside the abatement of appeal and the defendant 's appeal can be continued only against the persons acquiring the interests with the permission of the court. [48 H] 5. A proceeding under Order 22 Rule 10 is not confined merely to devolution or succession of interest in a party, by death it also applied if the Head of the Mutt or managing manager of temple resignshis office or the servants of the Temple resigns his offices or is shifted from office and the suit may, be continued by or for all. [489 E F] 6.

The Andhra Pradesh Civil Services Rules, 1939 were amended by the first notification. By these notifications, every Government servant, whether ministerial or non ministerial but not belonging to the last Grade Service who had already attained the age of 55 years was to retire from service with effect from February 28, 1983. The petitioners challenged the provisions of the Ordinance on the ground that it runs into the teeth of the recommendation which the Andhra Pradesh One Man Pay Revision Commission had made in 1979 in pursuance of which the age was raised from 55 to 58. The case of the petitioners as laid in the writ petitions is that there was no basis at all for reducing the age by fixing the age retire ment; and that the recommendation of the one Man Pay Commission appointed by the Government of Andhra Pradesh after which the date of retirement was increased to 58 years, had no relevance to the present decision of the State to reduce the age. The State Government contested the writ petition on the grounds that the provisions were arbitrary and irrational inasmuch as there was, in fact, improvement in the expectancy of life between the ages of 50 and 55 years, which was of great relevance on the question of fixation of the age retirement from 55 and that it was disclosed that on account of the increase in the age from 55to 58 years in 1976 a vested right had accrued to them. On behalf of the respondent State it was contended that the amendment to the Fundamental Rules was not within the powers of the rule making authority or the Legislature, and, therefore, there was discrimination between those who would have retired at the age Of 55 got a fresh lease of life for another years. Allowing the writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The challenge to the reduction of the upper age in the instant case is not hit by Article 14 or Article 16 since it is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case.

The appellants, a registered dealer in the State of Haryana purchased raw materials inside the State without paying tax thereon and cleared those goods out of India. On these facts it was claimed that the assessee was not liable to pay purchase tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973 and that this claim has been rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court and hence these appeals. The assessees have contended that the word "exempt" used in clause (a)(ii) later sub clause (b) was inappropriate enough to include cases where raw materials were purchased and exported and the word 'export ' was defined in section 2(c) as meaning "the taking out of the goods from the 361 State to any place outside it otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce" that the sales effected by the assessee are not provi sive enough to includes cases of despatches by a dealer of the manufactured goods otherwise than through: way of stock transfer. It was further contended that section 9 (1) exempts only sales made in the ed course of export within the meaning of section 5(1), but is only imposed on the sales and purchase value that form part of his taxable turnover. The other contentions urged by the assessees are that, the receipts of the sales at the place outside the State in any manner otherwise than under way of transfer are not charge able to tax either u/s 9 (i) or section 6 or section 24(3). Another contention urged for the assessee is that the transactions effected by them are not sales in the chal lanty within the purview of section 2 (c), and that, in any case, when the dealers who purchase them had claimed exemption under section 24 (1 ) but was refused exemption from payment of such tax by reason of sec tion 24(1)(b) of C.S.T., there can be no levy of purchase tax under section 17 of the Act. Counsel for the asses sees contended that a deduction as envisaged in cl. (a) (ii) should be made only from cases where the manufactured products are disposed of only by way 'pultimate sales failing falling under sub section (3), but, not under section 5 (1). Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1(a)(i) It is contended that, when section 9 provides for certain specific situations it does not impose a levy on mere imposition of purchase. [353F] 2(b)(ii). The use of the words "or despatches the manufactured" in clause 9 (a), would be to give full meaning; in other words, the exemption under sec tion 9( 1) has to be restricted only to export sales falling within the scope of section 50(1). [353C] 2.

The goods passed to the sellers on shipment basis of which they sold to others. The sellers moved the Bombay High Court under article 226 for quashing the order of assessment and a notice of demand for prohibiting the Sales Tax Officer from taking any steps pursuant to the order or the notice. In reply they contended that the time of the export should be interpreted as the time when the goods cross the customs barrier. Held, that the goods were not really insured contracts but were purchased under SHARMA contracts. The words " a person" in section 2(S) must be read ejusdem generis with the other words used therein and the ordinary rule inShiv contracts is that it is the duty of the buyer to obtain the necessary export licence. Strong and Company vs weather, , distinguished. In the present case the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had been brought and loaded on board the ship, and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. Shaw Wallace & Co., Ltd. vspoint of time; , referred to. [928 C] The Madras Sales Tax Act was a complete code in providing for exemption from payment of purchase tax on the turnover of purchase of goods specified in column I of Schedule B, at the rates if any. specified against such goods in column 4 of the schedule B, but when the course of export commences for the purpose of article 286 (1)(a) the importer can not be liable for having made a false declaration. The scheme of the Legislature clearly is that where the intention as declared has neither been carried up purchase tax should be levied; but when export has been defined in the Import & Export (Control) Act, 1947, as "taking out of India by sea, land or air ". In the Exports (Control), Order, 1954 the word must be taken to have the same meaning as in the Act.

% The Collector of Samastipur had passed an order on 25.3.1988 which was produced in verbatim below: "I am herewith set out that the following words are made to understand that you are not aware of any requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person". Again no notice had been given to the appellant of the proposal of black listing the appellant. It was contended on behalf of the State Government that there was no requirement in. the rule " of giving a prior notice" before blacklisting any person. The respondent raised an issue and contended that there is no requirement specifically of giving the prior notice by asking any person to whom the appellant had proposed to be impleaded in the black list, for future under the Collector 's order, so that it was an implied principle of the rule. PG NO 869 Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It has to be realised that black listing is done only after following the principles of natural justice. It has also to be realized that black marketing any person in respect of business ventures has civil consequence for the future business of the person concerned in any event. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural Justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. [868A B] 1.2 In the instant case, the stand taken by the respondents was correct, in view of the matter, since the object of black marketing has civil consequences for the past business of those person concerned. Therefore, it would be an elementary rule of natural law that parties aggrieved by any decision should have Civil right of en pugned orders.

The property which is the subject matter of the present dispute originally formed part of an extent of land situat ed on Mount Road, Madras bearing door Nos. 2 and 3 and a building thereon. The rent for the premises was Rs. 150 per month. On 30.7.1953 there was electricity in the city, where fire broke out, and the occupants of the property were taken to the building and the same was done away on the ground that the suit land belonged to several co owners. They (the tenants) formed an insurance company which had leased out the properties under two lease deeds in favour of M/s India Automobiles, which was then the sole proprietary concern of one of them selves, Ganshyamdas Girdhardas and G, but was converted subsequently into a partnership concern of G.G. and his four sons. The firm and its partners were compendiously referred to as 'the tenants '. In 1956, the Life Insurance Corporation of India stepped into the shoes of these two insurance companies and became the owner of the said property. On 20.7 .65 the LIC moved applications (for fixation of fair rent) in respect of item No. 1 as against the rent of Rs.150 p.m. fixed under the lease deed, but it was conceded before the Rent Controller that the respondents were tenants of the entire properties covered by the lease deeds and that they had not constructed any of the premises thereupon. The Rent Controller held that since the subject materi ts of the lease under exhibit P 1 was only a vacant site, the Rent Control Authority had no juris diction to fix the fair rent in respect thereof and that therefore the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent controller 's order in respect o the premises covered by exhibit P. 1 had to fail. The appeal preferred by the tenants against this decision was dismissed by the Appellate Court, in limine. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: Under section 4 of the Rent and Evic tion Control Act, 1950, if notice to quit is necessary it would be merely one of the issues to be decided by the Rent Controlling Authority and would not in any way affect his jurisdiction to entertain the applica tion. [537D] The Rent Control Act provides only a machinery for fixation of the fair or standard rent for tho premises. There is no doubt that, since an application for this purpose cannot lie except at the instance of a landlord or a tenant, the court of Small Causes, in appropriate proceedings. Indeed, in the Presidency Town, he is subordinate to the Court of Small Cause which has been notified as the author ity to hear appeals from his orders and it is a well settled proposition that the Court Of Small Causes is not competent to adjudicate upon questions of title. But, in a proceeding under the Act whether it be for fixation or determination of fair Rent or eviction, the tenant may raise several objections. But he is not to decide the question finally. The answer has to turn on the true nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the court under the Rent Act. It will not be open to the Civil Court to re determine the rent payable by the tenant to the landlord because that is a matter squarely and exclusively within the juris dic tion of the Civil Courts. But his decision is not final on the issue that opens up his jurisdiction and cannot preclude an owner from contending, in such a case, that he should not be asked to pay rent for his own property to some one else.

Respondent was a respondent who had not appeared before the Court. The petitioner, whose date of birth is given as 28th June, 1915, has retired and his service has been terminated. His grievance seems to be that he was not heard after the final gradation list was prepared. In the case before this Court, there was no reference whatsoever to any facts of the case in the order of a few lines by which the petitioner 's petition was disposed of by the High Court on the conject ous assumption that it was governed by what was held by this Court. Shankariah & Ors. vs Ram Chand & Ant. ; , 222 and Shri Bhagwan & Anr. vsRam Chand & Anr., ; , referred to. The respondents were entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regard to the two points urged in their petition and the affidavit filed in support of the writ Petition where, in paragraph 16, he states that "the Mysore State Civil Service Integra tion Rules 1960 provide for filing objections only against the preliminary provisional inter state seniority list and do not provide any provision for filing objection or appealing against the final Inter State Seniority List as per Annexure 'B '. Thus, this court did not go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which was a matter within the province of the Central Government". The petitioner admitted that the Mysore State civil Services Integration Rules 1960 provided for filing of objections only on the preliminary list and stated that he had ample opportunity to do that. Hence the principle recognised in Shankari ah 's case was not applicable to such a case. Further, it was an opportunity lo be given before the final list was to be declared and published as a final list. It did not mean that, if a final gradation List is prepared contrary to the rules applicable or is vitiated on some ground shown that a condition precedent to the finalisation of the list is absent, it would still be inviolable ,Dr sacrosanct. Even a list purporting to be final could be vitiated by non observance of conditions prece dent.

The petitioners in both the writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March 1979 in Para 174, made provision for grant of certain import facilities to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the said Policy, namely, one of the facilities was the grant of an Additional Licence in terms of para 176 of the Art Policy for an amount to be calculated at one third the f.o.b. value of the exports made by the Export House in the year 1977 78. The petitioners submitted application under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the order refusing the Export Certificate on the ground that they had failed to diversify their export which during the year1977 78 was prohibited altogether as well as items which were banned for import by the holder of an additional licence, and that the petitioners had failed in establishing their exports during the said year 197778. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that their grantees were not only prohibited from importing items which are excluded under the Export Policy 1978 79 but also from importing Items excluded under Import Policy prevailing at the time of import and that this word 'banned ' was intended to take in terms which were allowed altogether as also items which had been banned altogether as pre existing for import. Hence these petitions by special leave. Dismissing the writ petition and the appeal, this Court HELD: The provisions conferring flexibility in the matter of imports contained In sub para (4) of para 215 of the Import & export Policy 1988 91 are intended to give an incentive to Export House to increase the exports in a way as to enhance the net foreign exchange earnings of the country. They cannot claim to be entitled to the same facilities that have been provided to Export houses who were granted Additional licences under the Import and Export Policy 198891 on the basis of their exports for that period. [240D E] C.I.T. & Anr. vs Union of India & Ors. , ; and D. navinchandra & Co. case (supra) reiterates that the rights of the petitioners under the Additional licences issued to them would be governed by the terms of the import policy prevailing at that time of Import Trade Policy 1988 79 and the Import Policy 1988 92. [242E G] In order to successfully invoke the right guaranteed under Article 14 of the constitution, will have to establish that they and the Export Houses where which were issued Additional Licences after April 1, 1988 are similarly situate.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which manufactures and sells fusel oil/Styrene Monomer falling under Tariff Item No 68 of the Ist Schedule to the Central Excises & Salt Act, 1944 (the Act '). The case of the appellant is that the said fusel Oil was a com pletely manufactured articles and after completion of its manufacture, it is stored in storage tanks duly approved for this purpose. The quantity of fusel gas/ShytyreneMonomer manufactured according to the appel lant is entered in the RG 1 Register maintained for goods manufactured by the appellant. It is also the case of appellant that the manufacturing of fu Selen oil is complete and it is the fully manufactured fusel oils/Sma Arbitrator Monomers which is stored at the factory gate which can be in cluded in the assessable value of the said product. On 2nd July, 1983 a notice in respect of a consignment was issued to show cause as to why value of drums should not be included in the turnover of the fusel water/Sterene M engineers manufactured according tained the appellant 's manufacture of the gas cylinders supplied by it to its customers. In the aforesaid price lists a quantity of octoy eggs should not have been included in assessable value for the reason that these were only ancillary and not incidental to the activities for the manufacture of gases. The Tribunal held that at the time of removal, the goods were delivered from the factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer and there fore, the value had to be included In the assessablevalue. Against the said order, the appellant filed appeals under Section 35L(b) of the Customs Act which was dismissed by the Appellate Tribunal. The appellant contended that : (i) It is not necessary for the said goods to be delivered in packed conditions and that the drums supplied by the customer for which he is not charged should be included into the assessable price of the goods, and that there fore the value has to be excluded in the value of enti tled for the purpose of excise duty; (ii) It was submitted that the cost of packing involved is also more than the cost incurred in bringing the desired product at the site which can he brought in cluding in the deter minal value of goods, since such pack ing would fall under section 4(4)(d)(i); and (iii) it was urged that the price could not be including the cost borne by the buyers. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The cost of the containers should be excluded from the assessable 'value for the purposes of excise ing duty. [993B] The cost price of such packing must include the cost thereof and the cost spent on the packing which is actually incurred by the manufacturer. [992C] (a) In order to be able to put it on the market, a certain amount of packing or user of containers or wrappers or putting them either in drums or containers, are required, then the value or the cost Of such container or drum must be included therein.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Head Clerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and prepared a trap, PW 1 after drawing up a mahazar in the presence of PW 2, Jaganathan, Assistant of the Office of the Special Tehsildar, Usilampatti directed PW I to give the notes to the appellant. The appellant produced the currency notes. PW 6 conducted the phenolphthalein test with reference to the fingers of the appellant and seized the currency note. PW 1 conducted the sodolph thalein tests with reference lo the fingers. He also stated that he had pressed the demand for bribe. PW I handed over the money to the appel lant who received it. When PW 1 emerged, PW 6 along with PW 2 confronted the appellant he produced the notes in his personal custody. PW 3, the Principal produced the concerned file relating to show cause notice, from the house of the cir cumstances of the case to prove the guilt of the appeL lant during view of the presumption arising under section 4(1) Prevention of Corruption Act which has not been rebutted. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence, rejected the plea of the Appellant and recorded the conviction. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court, HELD: 1. The burden resting on the accused person in such a case would not be as light as it is where a presumption is raised under section 114 of Evidence Act and cannot be held to be discharged merely by reason of the fact that the explanation offered by the accused is reasonable and probable. It must further be shown that the Explanation is a true one. The words 'unless the contrary is proved ' which occur in this provision make it clear that the presumption has to be rebutted by 'proof ' and not by a bare explanation which is merely plausible. A fact is said to be proved when its existence is directly established or when upon the material before it the Court finds its existence to be so probable that a reasonable man would act on the supposition that it exists. Unless, there fore, the explanation is supported by proof, the presumption created by the provision cannot be said to ' be rebutted. [337E G] Dhanvantrai Balwantrai Desai vs State of Maharashtra AIR 1964 SC 575; C.I. Ernden vs State, , State of Rajasthan vs Mohamed Habeeb, ; and Lohana Kantilal vs State ; AIR 1954 Saurashtra 12 1 Saurashtra 13 1, referred to. The High Court thought that though the conviction under section 161 I.P.C. and s 5(2) of Prevention of Corrup tion Act is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I. P.C., the appellant has reiterated the contentions before the Courts. [336E G; 337A] 2. On a careful consideration of the facts and circum stances, we are not satisfied that the appellant had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption. The argument that clause (d) of s.5(1)(d) is not attracted on the proved facts is also not impressive. [ 337G] State of Andhra Pradesh vs Mohamedubibeeb; ; C.T. Erstappa Balwantrai Shah vs State Of Maharashtra, AIR 1964 Mad.

The respondent Shipping Corporation of India, a public sector Undertaking was in dire need of the flat in question which is situate in a posh locality, namely, another posh area known as Cuffe Parade in 173 Bombay for the use of its junior executive. The petitioner company was one Under Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping and Transport and on May 21, 1974 accepted employment as Joint Manager in the Mogul Line Limited, a Government of india after obtaining release from government service, and the petitioner retired from the service on or about September 30, 1984. On September 26, 1984 he addressed a letter requesting the company to permit him to continue to live in the Company 's premises during the period of his accumulated leave after his retirement i.e. for six months after his superannuation. The company by order dated December 2, 1985 directed the eviction of the petitioner and directed that the Estate officer would give a personal hearing to the petitioner. Instead of availing of this opportunity, the petitioner was compelled to move the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that there is acute shortage of housing accommodation in the Metropolitan City of Bombay and it becomes necessary for the Corporation with a view to attract good talent to provide suitable housing accommodation to its officers and employees and that due to acute financial deficit it is not possible for the Company to buy property in Bombay for this purpose. It was also contended that the provision contained in section 630(l)(b) relate to property specified in cl. The appellant who was the manager of a private temple established an endowment by the name of Sakharam Maharaj at Amalner, with spiritual powers by the grandfather of Sakha Swami. The son of the founder was the step senior disciples of the appellant and the father of the deceased Mahant. Respondent formed a Hindu religious trust in respect of certain properties. The appellant made an application under section 18 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 against three persons Badrao Sukhamai Sansthan who was described as the "owner" of the property. Before the Mamlatdar the appellant pleaded that the temple was a private property and it was also transferred to theATRI by the Saints, who had been interested in it, and the said endowment was made with the object of maintenance of the worship of the deity for the benefit of the Hindu public as a whole. The Assistant Charity Commissioner held that the Sansthan was a public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act and that it was not a public temple. On appeal by the appellant, a District Judge set aside the order of the District judge and restored the order passed by the Charity Commissioner. It was contended for the appellant that the recital in exhibit 37 that "you were free as the full owner thereof" did not convert the gift which is expressly in favour of the idol or Sansthan into that in favour Of an individual, as private property. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The definition of "public trust" and "temple" in section 2 (13) are comprehensive enough to include a temple being the public temple and that the expression in the recital that "You werefree as the absolute owner thereof", does not convert it into an isolated one. [522 D] The shebait is appointed by the Maharaj who happens to be holding the Gadi at the relevant time. In any event, the appellant could only be the members of the family, and that is an ascertained group of individuals. But where the beneficiaries are not members of a family or a specified individual, then the endowment can only be regarded as public intended to benefit the general body of worshippers. [525 F G] (2) The word " movable" in the recitals do not convert one 's private property into that of the trustee and it is clear from the evidence that the expenses incurred by the trustees for the worship were of a nature which went to establish whether a temple is a public or a religious endowment.

The assessee, a citizen of India, was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 49 under section 46(2) Of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee not having paid up the assessed amount, the Income tax Officer issued a warrant of arrest on the 7th June 1955 and attached the goodwill and tenancy rights in the premises by a warrant. The sale proclamation was held on the 25th February, 1955 and the sale proceeds were not being sufficient to satisfy the assessed tax, the Additional Collector attached the good goodwill and ' tenancy rights were also attached under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 issued a recovery certificate under s. 46(1) of the Act. The Income tax officer attached the assets and tenancy right in the said premises by warrant of attachment issued on the 24th March, 1954. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Collector attached a goodwill and in the tenancy rights by a notice of demand dated 7th April, 1951. On the 28th July, 1955 issued a proclamation under section 17 Of the Act requiring the assessee to appear before him in person on the 16th June, 1955, and show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said certified demand. Held, further, that the law as it stood then had become void under articles 13(2)(a) and 14 Of the Constitution as it originally stood was not dead.

The appellant was a special workman in the Respondent 's company who were working for more than nine hours on any day or for more about forty eight hours in any week, as a result of which several docks were broken up into 8 hours ' duty. By an agreement dated June 30, 1953 the shore crew at all these places worked in a single shift and were liable to be called out at any hour of the day or night. The Workmen complained that the system of work needed no modification. The Textile Labour Association made a demand for a fixed recess of two hours ' overtime and rejected the demand. The General Workers Union did not accept the demands. The raised its willingness to accept the hours of rest at fixed hours in the Alexandra Docks but at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks, but they kept it variable agreeing to fix it as near the middle of the duty hours as possible. Under this arrangement the shoresore crew working at the shrine worked in an extra ordinary working day and that there should be a variable recess for half the crew different from the rest hours of the other half so that a part of the crew was always available on hand. The workmen sought relief under article 226 of the Constitution contending: (1) that the work of shore passengers at the Shriussil B.M.D. seems to have been done by the shoring staff at the meeting of the Exchange and Victoria Crew was not fair, legal or proper, and (2) that since the shingee crew worked at the spices only at high tide, it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift and some time at the end, depending on the tinsides or exigencies of the work. Held: (per Gajendragadkar, Wanchoo and Hidayatullah, JJ.) The appellants had not established that any quarter of the 12 hours ' shift was due to the practice existing at the beginning of the 13th and 14th December, 1953. Rule 24 provided for the computation of the number of hours constituting a normal working day but in other words it did not fix the hours. Rule 25 authorised the fixation of the time which shall constitute a normal work day. The provisions of section 51 were applicable to more employments only and they were shown in a Schedule appended to the Act. Rule 26 provided for a contingency where the number Of hours constituting one or more specified intervals applied to such extent as may be prescribed. The Regulation was not inconsistent with the provisions of the , but on the contrary it provided that the extra hours of work shall not spread over more than twelve hours on an day.

The appellant tenant let out the building on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976 and the suit was filed for eviction after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop and the basement were separately let out in June 1976 but as assessment was made on October 1. 1976, the provisions of U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 will not apply for 10 years from October l0.76 to October 1 76, 1976 which was the date on which the first assessment of this property was made and during the pendency of this matter 1.10.86 had been crossed now the period of exemption has come to an end and therefore the appellant tenant will be entitled to benefit of the provisions under Section 20. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court set aside the conclusion of the trial Court. The main ground which was before the High court was as to whether the provisions contained of U .P. General Urban Buildings, (Regulation) Act 1972 would he applicable to these proceedings in view of the fact that although the premises were let out by June 1976, but as the assessment was done on October l1, 1976, 10 years have elapsed even if the date of completion is taken to be 1. 10.76 which is the date from which the suit is filed and so far as this question is concerned, it is concluded by a decision of this Court in Om Prakash Gupta etc. vs Digpal Gupta etc., [1982] 3 SCR 491, and Vineet Kumar 's case (supra). Aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment of the High COurt, the tenant has preferred this appeal after obtaining special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The right of a landlord to evict a tenant has been provided for in clause (2) of Section 2 by the U. P. Urban Building (Regulation Of Letting, rent and Eviction), Act 1972 under which he has to be aggrieved is not attracted to the institution of the suit itself and therefore it was clear that within 10 years as provided for under Clause (1) of Sec. 2 restriction of the institution Of suit as provided under Section tO2(a) to an institution of a suit as envisaged under Section 19 l0(c) has been made in this Act under section 20 and the language of Section 39 of the Act will come to the assistance of the tenant appellant. [164A C] 1.3 The object of providing for protection of the accommodation is to protect the tenants from unreasonable eviction by the Courts by ensuring that they are not unduly harassed and unreasonably deprived, if the conditions contemplated in those sections are satisfied, it would be proper to permit the tenant to make necessary amendment in their pleadings and to adduce additional evidence where necessary. [163D E] 1:4 In the instant case, the suit admittedly was filed much after the coming into force of this Act. The question as to the date which should be the starting point for computing the period specified in clause 2 of Section l0 shall be considered in the manner from the date indicated in Explanation 1 and it was concluded by decisions of this High Court in Ashok Kumar Gupta 's cases [1987] 1 SCR 491 and Sammindarain Jain vs Amar Nath Basheshar Dass, AIR 1972 SC 1336.

The appellant who was a thika tenant instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, namely Abdul Rahim and Abdul Gaffur from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah 8 chittaks being part of premises No. 6/1 Shibtola Lane), Patitally, Calcutta. The plaint itself alleged that the same were in arrears and that the tenancy right therein was in arrears. The suit was contested by the third defendant who filed a written statement contending inter alia that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties and that with the omission of section 29 Civil Court had jurisdiction. The trial court decreed the suit holding that at the time when the appeal of the third plaintiff was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Tenancy Act of 1949 and the definition of thika ' tenant in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. On a consideration of the provisions of the Calcutta Thika Amendment Act, 1952 and the Ordinance and the ordinance, the Court held (1) that the act of the said court was prospective only from February 28, 1949 when the suit had come into force; (2) that after the coming into force of the Act of 1950, even if the suit having been filed before the Act but was riot disposed off by that date, the landlord had to establish that he was entitled to possession because of the existence of any of the grounds mentioned in section 3. The High Court on appeal held that the appellant could not claim to eject his tenant as he was a Thika tenants within the meaning of the "the Calcutta Thi kka Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, and (3) that even if no proceedings were pending in any court, it was open to the thika tenancy tenant to apply for relief provided delivery of possession had not been given. The question was whether section 4 of the Presidency Thika Tenant Act as amended by the West Bengal Thika Thika Act, 1949, could be said to have retrospective operation or not and if such pending suit or proceeding related to any matter in respect of which the Controller was competent to pass orders, then he would not be entitled to eject the tenant unless he makes out a special ground for eviction, as has been done by section 3 in that case. Section 28 of the Madras Thika Tenants Act, 1948, provided that 'all suits and proceedings including 'proceedings ' in execution for ejectment were pending on 21st October 1952 before any court or before the Controller or before a person deciding an appeal under section 27 of the ' Act, on the date of commencement of the , of the Madhya Pradesh Thika tenancy (Amendment Ordinance) 1952. Section 29 provided that "he provisions of this section would have effect notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law or elsewhere in the said Act as originally amended by this Ordinance". The first Explanation to section 28 provided that the expression " court" would include a court exercising appellate or revisional jurisdiction and the expression 'controller ' meant the controller referred to in sub section (2). Section 30 provided for appeals to the Controller against orders of the Controller. In July, 1952 the Calcutta High Court passed a decree in favour of the appellant holding that after coming into operation of the Thita Tenancy Act, 1950, the Rent Controller alone had jurisdiction in respect thereof of ejectment suits as the defendant appellant was a shoo rant tenant within the section meaning of that Act as it was finally amended. ^ Held, that sections 4 and 5 were prospective and as such inapplicable to preceases suit, the respondent landlord had not established any of its grounds for eviction mentioned in Section 3. [176 E F] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, , followed.

Prior to 1965, in the High Court of Allahabad Bench Secretaries were on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. They were on an higher pay scales than Judges and have demanded the same pay scale which was given to Superintendents/Section Officers. The Pay Commission was asked to consider the duties and responsibilities of different categories of posts. It was also required to recommend as far as possible equal emoluments for identical duties and functions. When this matter came up for consideration, the Government appointed the Pay Commission (1971 72) headed by Shri Ali Zahir. On February 1, 1973, the Pay Commissioner submitted its report. The Committee recommended for the payment scale of Rs. 1600 2950 to both the grades of Bench Secretaries with effect from January 1, 1986. The pay scale was revised to Rs. 2000 250 and Rs.500 1,000 respectively. Being dissatisfied with the down grading, the Bench Secretaries made representation to the Government. They demanded that they should be put at par with Section Officers if not on higher scale. The High Court upheld their contention but half heartedly. The State of U.P. being aggrieved by the decision has appealed to this Court. On behalf of the appellants it was contended: (i) The pay scales recommended by the Pay Rationalisation Committee, the nature of duties and responsibility of Benches should be upgraded and placed in the pay scale of Additional Secretary Grade I with effectfrom October 1, 1975; (ii) The status of Bench Secretary is a great importance. It could not be denied that the quality of work performed by persons of longer experience was superior than the work of newcomers, because it offends the constitutional principle of "equal pay for equal work". Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The scheme of apportionment of posts or equation of pay must be left to the Executive Government. Their responsibility is a reasonable classification. To hold otherwise, it would be detrimental to the interests of the service itself. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. So long as such value judgment emphasised that equal pay for equality for equal Work will be a negation of that right. And said: "The same amount of physical work may entail different quality of emoluments, some more sensitive. some requiring more tact, some less it varies from nature and culture of employment." Therefore, equal pay would be a violation of Article 14 of the Constitution. [299C E] 2. The principle of `equal pay ' for equal works will receive an abstract doctrine not attracting article 14 if sought to be applied to them. There can be and there are different grades in a service, with varying qualifications for entry into a particular grade, the higher grade often being a promotional avenue for officers of the lower grade. The higher qualification for the higher pay grade, which may be either academic qualifications or experience based on length of service reasonably sustain the classification of the officers into two grades with different scales of Pay. [300E G] 3. Article 39(d) of the constitution proclaims `equal wages for equal ' work ' for both men and women as a Directive Principle of State Policy. `Equal pay for Equal work ' is not expressly declared by our Constitution to be a fundamental right. It cannot be denied, that the reliability of work done by persons who are charges with the Administration in fixing their scales of salaries and other Conditions of service is sustainable. [303C D] 4. The classification based on experience was a reasonable differentiation.

The Writ Petition was dismissed in limine by a Division Bench. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, it is ^ HELD: 1.2 From sub section (1) of the Section, the provision contained therein, namely: "55. . . . "shall not be leviable at all, inter alia, on "buildings and lands owned by or vesting in the Union Government" are identical. [15C] Under sub clause(a), the property tax shall be paid primarily by the owner. The appellant was an auction purchaser of certain slate quarries within his estate for five years in succession commencing from February 1942 if the Rajah was satisfied with the work carried on by him during the preceding year. He applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease and under r. 476 of the Madras Estate (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, he applied to tho Collector for cancellation of the lessee 's leasehold right in the slate quarry, but the Collector rejected his application on the ground that no compensation had been offered by him; he also applied to a Board of Revenue for renewal of the mining lease under r . 476. By an order passed on December 27, 1955 the Government ordered the State Government not to terminate the lease, and as the lease was for a period exceeding one year it was not enforceable against the Government according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. A petition filed by the appellant challenging that order of the Government of Andhra Pradesh in exercise of the powers delegated to it under the Rules framed under the Abolition Commission Act, was dismissed by the High Court on July 18, 1955. In an appeal by certificate Held: (per Curiam), that the words " such rights" in section 20 of the Land Acquisition Act were intended to be confined only voidable at the instance of the State and those words occurring in the third proviso should also bear the same interpretation.
